adj-list-hash-optimization.text: Replacing adjacency lists with hash sets gives amortized O(1) adjacency test and edge removal, improving over the default O(|V|) adjacency test of plain adjacency lists

adj-list-space-complexity.text: Adjacency list representation uses O(|V| + |E|) space and is the preferred representation for sparse graphs where |E| << |V|²

adj-list-vs-matrix-adjacency-test.text: Adjacency test is O(|V|) for adjacency list but O(1) for adjacency matrix — a fundamental complexity tradeoff between the two representations

adj-matrix-add-vertex-cost.text: Adding a vertex to an adjacency matrix costs O(|V|²) due to matrix resizing, compared to O(1) for an adjacency list

adj-matrix-space-complexity.text: Adjacency matrix representation uses O(|V|²) space and is preferred for dense graphs or when O(1) edge existence testing is needed

adt-abstraction-enables-optimization-spe.text: The ADT abstraction layer enables systematic implementation optimization across fundamentally different data types: queues admit progressively stronger implementations (circular buffer → two-stack → real-time) along the amortized-to-worst-case axis, while priority queues admit progressively faster implementations (unsorted array → binary heap → Fibonacci heap) along the constant-factor-to-asymptotic axis — in both cases, the fixed abstract interface permits internal optimization without client-side changes.

justifications.label: Queues and priority queues both demonstrate that fixed ADT interfaces enable systematic internal optimization along different axes

adt-layer-concretizes-dual-universal-mec.text: The ADT layer is the concrete realization through which the canon's two universal mechanisms become computationally operative: stacks and queues specialize traversal (DFS and BFS respectively, partitioning the structural exploration space), while priority queues specialize ordering (converting the ordering invariant into optimal extraction for greedy algorithms) — creating a clean mapping from abstract mechanism to concrete computational infrastructure that is both complete and non-redundant.

justifications.label: The abstract dual mechanisms (ordering and traversal) need concrete realization; the ADT layer provides exactly that through stack/queue/PQ specialization.

adt-paradigm-infrastructure-complete.text: The canon's ADT layer achieves both horizontal completeness (three ADTs — stack, queue, PQ — span the full paradigm hierarchy from structural exploration through traversal to greedy optimization) and vertical optimization depth (each ADT admits systematic internal optimization along its own axis without client changes) — making ADTs simultaneously the paradigm infrastructure and its own optimization target.

justifications.label: Three ADTs span paradigms (depth-6) + ADT abstraction enables optimization (depth-3) = horizontally complete and vertically optimizable infrastructure layer

adt-property-axes.text: Abstract data types vary on two axes: ordered vs unordered (elements have explicit sequence or not), and unique vs non-unique (duplicates allowed or not). List = ordered + non-unique; Set = unordered + unique; Map = unique keys; Multiset/Bag = unordered + non-unique.

aho-corasick-instantiates-trie-dfa-equiv.text: Aho-Corasick's multi-pattern matching automaton is the canonical practical instantiation of the trie-DFA equivalence: the trie provides the tree-shaped deterministic automaton for simultaneous pattern matching, and failure links extend it to handle mismatches without backtracking — achieving linear-time multi-pattern search where KMP handles only single patterns.

justifications.label: Aho-Corasick concretely realizes the theoretical trie-DFA equivalence for multi-pattern search

aho-corasick-multi-pattern.text: Aho-Corasick searches for multiple patterns simultaneously using a trie-based automaton, unlike KMP which searches for a single pattern. KMP avoids re-examination of matched characters; Boyer-Moore achieves sublinear performance in practice.

algorithms-canon-structure-meets-meta-te.text: The algorithms canon converges on two interlocking dimensions: structural efficiency (graph paradigm coverage + hardware-bridging tree implementations) and meta-analytical techniques (DP for optimization, amortized analysis for feasibility guarantees) — structure determines WHAT is computable efficiently, meta-techniques prove WHY the guarantees hold.

justifications.label: Depth-7 capstone unifying the structural and analytical pillars of algorithmic knowledge

algorithms-pillars-connected-not-paralle.text: The algorithms canon's two pillars (graph optimization and sorting/computation) are not independent domains but a connected directed system: sorting theory generates the priority queue abstraction that graph algorithms consume for optimization (Dijkstra, Prim), establishing a concrete dependency where mastery of sorting foundations — including the comparison-sort lower bound, the PQ-sort equivalence, and non-comparison circumvention — is prerequisite to understanding graph algorithm performance tiers.

justifications.label: One depth-6 establishes two complete pillars, the other shows a concrete pipeline between them — their combination reveals the pillars are connected, not parallel

algorithms-structure-optimization-pillar.text: Algorithmic problem-solving rests on two complementary pillars: graph algorithms achieve complete paradigm coverage from traversal through greedy to DP-based optimization, while tree data structures bridge theoretical optimality to hardware efficiency across the memory hierarchy — together ensuring that asymptotically optimal algorithms exist AND execute efficiently on real machines.

justifications.label: Graph algorithms provide the "what to compute" and trees provide the "how to compute it fast" — completeness on both axes

all-pairs-negative-weight-augmented.text: Floyd-Warshall provides the complete all-pairs negative-weight solution: it is the all-pairs member of the negative-weight algorithm portfolio (complementing single-source Bellman-Ford), and its practical augmentations (path reconstruction via predecessor matrix, transitive closure via Warshall's Boolean specialization) extend its utility beyond raw distances — all within the same O(|V|³) KIJ loop structure.

justifications.label: Floyd-Warshall is the augmented all-pairs counterpart to Bellman-Ford's single-source role

amortized-accounting-credit-nonneg.text: In the accounting method for amortized analysis, the accumulated credit must remain non-negative. This non-negativity constraint is what guarantees the amortized cost is an upper bound on actual cost.

amortized-analysis-both-enables-and-expl.text: Amortized analysis plays a unique dual analytical role at the paradigm peak: it is the prerequisite that makes the greedy graph algorithms achievable (validating Fibonacci heap bounds that power Dijkstra/Prim) and it is the explanatory framework that reveals how the canon's asymptotic crown achievements depend on co-evolution between analysis techniques and data structures — it simultaneously unlocks and accounts for optimal performance.

justifications.label: Paradigm-peak prerequisite (depth-5) + enabler-and-driver dual role (depth-5) = amortized analysis as the single analytical technique that both creates and explains the canon's performance ceiling

amortized-analysis-bridges-two-mastery-c.text: Amortized analysis connects two of the three independent mastery competences: it supports paradigm awareness by serving as the analytical prerequisite that validates greedy algorithms at the paradigm hierarchy's peak (amortized reasoning underpins Fibonacci heap guarantees and thus optimal Dijkstra/Prim), and its analytical framework for evaluating data structure performance guarantees is relevant to hardware-aware implementation choices — leaving correctness verification as the competence least mediated by amortized reasoning among the three.

justifications.label: Amortized analysis spans paradigm awareness and hardware codesign, two of three mastery dimensions

amortized-analysis-def.text: Amortized analysis averages the running times of operations in a sequence over that sequence, rather than analyzing the worst-case cost of individual operations. It is a worst-case technique (no probabilistic assumptions) applied to sequences of operations.

amortized-analysis-dual-role-enabler-and.text: Amortized analysis plays dual roles in the algorithms canon: as analytical enabler, it validates the asymptotically optimal graph algorithms (Fibonacci heaps for O(1) decrease-key powering Dijkstra/Prim, union-find's near-constant operations powering Kruskal); as design methodology, it drives the universal amortized-to-worst-case refinement pattern across multiple ADT families (Fibonacci → Brodal queues, two-stack → real-time queues, standard → optimized union-find) — making it both the technique that justifies current optimal algorithms and the framework that guides their future improvement.

justifications.label: Enables optimal graph algorithms (justification role) + drives ADT refinement pattern (design methodology role)

amortized-analysis-enables-fundamental-g.text: Amortized analysis is the enabling analytical technique for three fundamental data structure guarantees that would appear impossible under worst-case analysis alone: dynamic arrays achieve O(1) append despite O(n) resize events, two-stack queues achieve O(1) dequeue despite O(n) transfers, and union-find achieves near-constant O(α(n)) operations that make Kruskal's MST edge-sort-dominated. In each case, amortized analysis proves that expensive operations are rare enough to not affect the per-operation bound.

justifications.label: Three independent depth-1 conclusions each depend on amortized analysis to establish guarantees that worst-case analysis cannot

amortized-analysis-enables-graph-optimiz.text: Amortized analysis is the theoretical enabler of optimal graph algorithms: it validates both Fibonacci heaps (O(1) amortized decrease-key powering O(|E| + |V| log |V|) Dijkstra/Prim) and union-find (O(α(n)) amortized operations powering edge-sort-dominated Kruskal), making the two cornerstone data structures of weighted graph optimization possible.

justifications.label: amortized guarantees enable both key graph data structures (Fibonacci heap + union-find)

amortized-analysis-enables-paradigm-peak.text: Amortized analysis is the analytical prerequisite for the highest performance tier of the algorithmic paradigm hierarchy: the greedy graph algorithms (Dijkstra, Prim, A*) that sit at the paradigm peak rely on Fibonacci heap O(1) amortized decrease-key, which only amortized analysis can validate — without this analytical technique, the paradigm hierarchy's optimal implementations would be computationally more expensive and the gap between theory and practice wider.

justifications.label: Amortized analysis (d4) validates the data structures that make greedy graph algorithms (d4) achieve their theoretical optima — it doesn't just describe performance, it enables the paradigm peak.

amortized-and-memoization-dual-efficienc.text: The algorithms canon employs two distinct bridging mechanisms that convert computationally expensive patterns into efficient ones at different abstraction levels: memoization bridges recursion and DP by converting exponential multiple-recursion into polynomial dynamic programming (algorithmic bridging), while amortized analysis bridges simple and optimal data structures by validating that occasional expensive operations in Fibonacci heaps and union-find yield efficient amortized bounds (analytical bridging) — parallel mechanisms operating on algorithms and data structures respectively.

justifications.label: Memoization and amortized analysis are parallel bridging mechanisms: one converts expensive algorithms, the other validates expensive data structure operations

amortized-coevolution-enables-graph-crow.text: Amortized analysis serves as a unifying analytical framework behind the asymptotically efficient MST and shortest path algorithms: union-find's path compression and rank heuristics yield a near-constant O(α(n)) amortized bound that makes Kruskal's algorithm edge-sort-dominated, while Fibonacci heap's O(1) amortized decrease-key supports O(|E| + |V| log |V|) Dijkstra/Prim — in both cases, amortized analysis is what validates these per-operation bounds, linking the two cornerstone data structures of weighted graph optimization to a shared analytical technique.

justifications.label: Union-find's demonstrated analysis-structure co-evolution (d3) and amortized analysis's enabling role for graph optimization (d4) combine to show that co-evolution is the mechanism by which amortized analysis powers the graph optimization crown.

amortized-coevolution-extends-to-queue-d.text: The co-evolutionary relationship between amortized analysis and specialized data structures — observed in the graph optimization crown (Fibonacci heaps + union-find) — extends to the queue ADT family: the same pattern of amortized guarantees enabling simpler implementations that are later refined to worst-case optimal drives the progression from two-stack queues (amortized O(1)) to real-time queues (worst-case O(1) via lazy evaluation).

justifications.label: The amortized-to-optimal co-evolutionary pattern extends from graph crown algorithms down to queue ADT design

amortized-fibonacci-heap-synergy.text: Amortized analysis is the indispensable theoretical tool for Fibonacci heaps: without amortized reasoning, the O(1) decrease-key that makes Dijkstra/Prim edge-dominated would appear to be O(log n), collapsing the asymptotic advantage over binary heaps and eliminating the performance tier separation in graph algorithms.

justifications.label: Amortized analysis doesn't just validate Fibonacci heaps — it is the only analytical framework that can see their advantage

amortized-not-average-case.text: Amortized analysis is NOT average-case analysis: it makes no assumptions about input distribution. Average-case analysis assumes inputs are not 'bad'; amortized analysis is worst-case analysis for a sequence of operations rather than for individual operations.

amortized-potential-formula.text: In the potential method: amortized cost = immediate cost + change in potential. The potential is a function of the data structure's state, formalizing the 'saved credit' concept from the accounting method.

amortized-refinement-spans-adt-hierarchy.text: The amortized-to-worst-case refinement pattern is a universal design progression spanning multiple ADT families: priority queues progress from Fibonacci heaps (O(1) amortized insert/decrease-key) to Brodal queues (O(1) worst-case), and queues progress from two-stack (O(1) amortized) to real-time (O(1) worst-case via lazy evaluation), demonstrating that amortized bounds systematically identify the target for worst-case refinement.

justifications.label: Both queues and priority queues exhibit the same amortized→worst-case progression, establishing it as a cross-ADT design principle

amortized-requires-sequence-knowledge.text: Amortized analysis requires knowledge of which series of operations are possible. It is most commonly applied to data structures with persistent state, where a worst-case operation alters state so the worst case cannot recur for a long time.

amortized-tarjan-1985.text: Amortized analysis was formally introduced by Robert Tarjan in his 1985 paper 'Amortized Computational Complexity'. Originally motivated by binary tree and union-find operations, it is now ubiquitous in algorithm analysis.

amortized-three-methods.text: Three equivalent methods for amortized analysis (all give correct upper bounds): (1) Aggregate method: T(n)/n, (2) Accounting method: assign amortized costs, accumulate non-negative credit, (3) Potential method: amortized cost = immediate cost + change in potential function of state.

amortized-to-worst-case-refinement-patte.text: In at least two data structure families, an amortized-optimal design precedes or accompanies a worst-case-optimal refinement: priority queues progress from Fibonacci heaps (O(1) amortized decrease-key) to Brodal queues and strict Fibonacci heaps (O(1) worst-case), and queues progress from the two-stack construction (O(1) amortized enqueue/dequeue) to real-time queues (O(1) worst-case via incremental lazy evaluation). In both cases the worst-case variant introduces additional mechanism — eager restructuring or schedule-driven incremental forcing — to eliminate the amortized debt.

justifications.label: Both PQ and queue families exhibit an amortized-first, worst-case-later refinement trajectory

analytical-methodology-triply-complete.text: The canon's analytical methodology addresses three complementary concerns: DP and amortized analysis serve as parallel meta-techniques for optimization design and efficiency validation respectively, while correctness verification methods partition by algorithmic paradigm (exchange arguments for greedy, recurrence correctness for DP, reject-function soundness for backtracking) — together these cover optimization, validation, and verification concerns, though the antecedents do not establish that this coverage is gap-free or that the listed verification methods are exhaustive across all paradigms.

justifications.label: Dual meta-techniques plus paradigm-specific verification span all analytical needs

architecture-grounds-both-pillars-and-ma.text: The three-layer computational architecture (physical substrates, ADTs, paradigms) appears to serve as a shared structural foundation that connects the canon's horizontal organization (two content pillars understood as distinct paths through the same layers) with its vertical skill framework (three mastery competences that align with the three layers), suggesting that content organization and pedagogical progression may be unified through this common infrastructure rather than being independent schemes.

justifications.label: Architecture is the shared root grounding both content pillars and mastery competences

architecture-mastery-verification-triple.text: The algorithms canon exhibits alignment across its organizational dimensions: the 2×2 content structure (two pillars × two meta-techniques) provides material that the three mastery competences operate on, with those competences mapping to computational architecture layers; meanwhile, verification methodology's paradigm-specific proof techniques (exchange argument, induction, precondition analysis) concretely instantiate the correctness competence within that mastery triad. Together these relationships suggest that content organization, skill development, and correctness verification are structurally reinforcing activities, though the claim of full isomorphism across all three dimensions goes beyond what the individual alignments establish.

justifications.label: Two independently derived alignment conclusions (mastery↔organization at depth 9, verification↔mastery at depth 8) share the same architectural substrate, revealing triple isomorphism

arms-length-recursion.text: Short-circuiting (arm's-length recursion) checks the base case before making the recursive call rather than after entering it, cutting function calls in half for perfect binary trees.

array-address-formula-1d.text: The address of element i in a 1D array is computed as address = B + c * i, where B is the base address and c is the stride (element size in bytes).

array-address-formula-kd.text: The address of an element in a k-dimensional array is address = B + c₁·i₁ + c₂·i₂ + … + cₖ·iₖ, requiring only k multiplications and k additions.

array-cache-misses.text: Iterating n array elements of size k with cache line size B requires ⌈nk/B⌉ cache misses — roughly B/k times better than random access patterns.

array-column-major-order.text: Column-major order (Fortran convention) stores elements of each column contiguously in memory; the first index varies fastest.

array-dimension-is-rank.text: The dimension (rank) of an array is the number of indices needed to select an element, not the total element count.

array-dope-vector.text: A dope vector (descriptor/stride vector) packs dimension d, base address B, and increments c₁…cₖ, serving as a complete handle for the array and enabling efficient slicing by manipulating metadata rather than copying data.

array-iliffe-vector.text: An Iliffe vector is a 1D array of pointers to 1D arrays, enabling jagged arrays where rows have different sizes; it is an alternative to true contiguous multidimensional layout.

array-implicit-tree-foundation.text: Arrays can serve as the implicit storage substrate for binary heaps and complete binary trees: binary heaps use 2i+1/2i+2 indexing (0-based) to eliminate pointer overhead, and complete binary trees use the same index formulas for parent-child navigation. Both exploit O(1) array access, with the address formula B + c·i as a underlying mechanism for element location.

justifications.label: O(1) array access enables implicit tree encodings that eliminate pointer overhead

array-layout-governs-cache-performance.text: Array memory layout (row-major C convention vs column-major Fortran convention) determines which iteration patterns achieve the optimal ⌈nk/B⌉ cache miss rate: iterating along the contiguous storage dimension exploits spatial locality, while cross-dimension iteration degrades to one useful element per cache line fetch — making layout choice a first-order performance decision.

justifications.label: storage order + cache line geometry = layout determines iteration performance

array-o1-access.text: Array store and select operations are worst-case O(1) time; this is the defining performance characteristic of arrays.

array-row-major-order.text: Row-major order (C convention) stores elements of each row contiguously in memory; the last index varies fastest.

array-universal-computational-substrate.text: Arrays serve dual roles in algorithm design: they provide direct O(1) access for data storage and act as the implicit storage substrate for tree-based structures (heaps, segment trees, complete binary trees) via address formulas that eliminate pointer overhead. In both roles, memory layout (row-major vs column-major) is a first-order performance decision — iterating along the contiguous storage dimension exploits spatial locality and can achieve the optimal ⌈nk/B⌉ cache miss rate, while cross-dimension iteration degrades to one useful element per cache line fetch.

justifications.label: Arrays serve as both direct storage and implicit tree substrate; cache layout governs performance in both modes

array-von-neumann-merge-sort.text: John von Neumann wrote the first array-sorting program (merge sort) in 1945 for EDVAC.

astar-admissible-heuristic.text: An admissible heuristic never overestimates the true cost to the goal; A* with an admissible heuristic is guaranteed to find an optimal solution

astar-completeness.text: On finite graphs with non-negative edge weights, A* is guaranteed to terminate and is complete (always finds a solution if one exists)

astar-completes-greedy-graph-paradigm.text: A*'s continuous optimality-speed tradeoff spectrum completes the greedy graph optimization paradigm for goal-directed search: it extends Dijkstra's optimal-but-uninformed approach with heuristic guidance, and weighted relaxation trades bounded sub-optimality for exponential speedup, making PQ-driven greedy algorithms applicable beyond shortest-path to informed search problems.

justifications.label: A* completes the greedy paradigm for goal-directed search but O(b^d) space limits applicability

astar-complexity.text: A* has worst-case time complexity O(|E| log |V|) = O(b^d) and space complexity O(|V|) = O(b^d), where b is branching factor and d is solution depth; space is the major practical limitation

astar-consistency-stronger.text: Consistency is strictly stronger than admissibility: consistency implies admissibility, but an admissible heuristic may not be consistent; without consistency, A* may need to expand some nodes more than once

astar-consistent-equiv-dijkstra.text: With a consistent heuristic, A* is equivalent to running Dijkstra's algorithm with reduced edge costs d'(x,y) = d(x,y) + h(y) - h(x)

astar-consistent-heuristic.text: A consistent (monotone) heuristic satisfies h(x) <= d(x,y) + h(y) for every edge (x,y); consistency implies admissibility but not vice versa; with consistency, no node is expanded more than once

astar-definition.text: A* is a graph traversal and pathfinding algorithm that finds the shortest path from source to goal in a weighted graph, using the evaluation function f(n) = g(n) + h(n)

astar-dijkstra-special-case.text: Dijkstra's algorithm is a special case of A* where h(x) = 0 for all x (uniform-cost search)

astar-eval-function.text: A* selects nodes to expand by minimizing f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g(n) is cost from start to n and h(n) is heuristic estimate from n to goal

astar-extends-dijkstra.text: A* extends Dijkstra's algorithm by adding heuristic guidance; Dijkstra's is the degenerate case with h(x) = 0

astar-history.text: A* was invented in 1968 by Peter Hart, Nils Nilsson, and Bertram Raphael at Stanford Research Institute as part of the Shakey the Robot project; it extended the Graph Traverser algorithm by adding g(n) to the heuristic h(n)

astar-ideal-informed-search.text: A* with a consistent heuristic is the theoretically ideal informed graph search: it is optimally efficient (no admissible algorithm expands fewer nodes) and guarantees shortest paths with no node re-expansion.

justifications.label: A*'s theoretical optimality is qualified by its O(b^d) space requirement which makes it impractical for very large search spaces, forcing practitioners to use bounded-memory variants like IDA*

astar-no-negative-weights.text: A* inherits Dijkstra's non-negative edge weight requirement: since A* extends Dijkstra with heuristic guidance, negative weights violate the greedy invariant that settled nodes have optimal costs.

justifications.label: depth-2 chain — A* extends Dijkstra which cannot handle negative weights

astar-open-set.text: A* uses a priority queue (open set/frontier) ordered by f(n) value; typically implemented as a min-heap. The node with lowest f(n) is expanded next

astar-optimal-efficiency.text: With a consistent heuristic, A* is optimally efficient: no A*-like algorithm expands fewer nodes on non-pathological problems (Dechter and Pearl, 1985)

astar-optimal-informed-search-on-finite-.text: A* with a consistent heuristic achieves optimal informed graph search on finite graphs: it is complete (guaranteed to find a solution), optimally efficient (no admissible algorithm expands fewer nodes), and equivalent to Dijkstra with reduced edge costs — the strongest possible guarantee for heuristic-guided pathfinding.

justifications.label: A*'s theoretical optimality holds unless its O(b^d) space makes it impractical for large state spaces

astar-optimality-speed-tradeoff-spectrum.text: A* supports an optimality-speed tradeoff: with a consistent heuristic (which implies admissibility) it guarantees optimal paths, though without consistency some nodes may need re-expansion; weighted A* with epsilon > 1 relaxes optimality for speed with a bounded suboptimality guarantee of at most epsilon times optimal cost — these two properties together suggest practitioners can tune the tradeoff by adjusting the heuristic strength or weighting.

justifications.label: Consistency and weighted relaxation define opposite ends of A*'s tunable optimality-speed axis

astar-practical-limitation.text: A*'s O(b^d) space complexity, requiring storage of generated nodes, can make it impractical for very large search spaces where the branching factor or solution depth is high

astar-weighted-relaxation.text: Weighted A* uses h_w(n) = epsilon * h(n) with epsilon > 1 to trade optimality for speed; guarantees solution cost at most epsilon times optimal (epsilon-admissible)

asymptotic-notation-three-layer-discipli.text: Rigorous complexity analysis requires three layers of asymptotic discipline: Big O's formal definition (existence of M such that |f| ≤ Mg), the distinction between upper bounds and tight bounds (Big O vs Theta), and the pursuit of tightness (preferring the tightest correct bound) — without all three, complexity claims are either technically meaningless, misleadingly loose, or asymmetrically informative.

justifications.label: Three Big O principles form a layered discipline from definition to tightness

augmented-tree-overlap-condition.text: In an augmented interval tree, each node stores max(high endpoint) of its entire subtree. Two intervals A and B overlap iff A_low <= B_high AND B_low <= A_high. This annotation enables pruning entire subtrees during queries.

augmented-trees-extend-bst-ordering-to-i.text: Augmented interval trees extend the BST ordering principle from point queries to interval queries: the BST ordering invariant handles point search/insert/delete via key comparison, while the subtree-max augmentation (max high endpoint per subtree) adds interval overlap detection at O(log n + m) — the same balanced tree substrate serves both point and range semantics through a single auxiliary annotation.

justifications.label: BST ordering extends from point operations to interval operations via a single augmentation

avl-asymmetric-modification-cost.text: AVL trees have asymmetric structural modification costs: insertion requires at most 1 rotation (O(1) rebalancing) while deletion may cascade O(log n) rotations, making AVL trees better suited for lookup-heavy than mutation-heavy workloads.

justifications.label: depth-2 — contrasting the derived rotation bounds reveals an insert/delete asymmetry

avl-balance-factor.text: Balance factor BF(X) = Height(RightSubtree(X)) - Height(LeftSubtree(X)). Only 2 bits per node needed to store it. BF < 0 is left-heavy, BF > 0 is right-heavy, BF = 0 is balanced.

avl-complexity.text: AVL tree operations: Search O(log n), Insert O(log n), Delete O(log n) -- all worst-case. Space O(n). These bounds hold for both amortized and worst case.

avl-definition.text: An AVL tree is a self-balancing binary search tree where the balance factor (height difference of child subtrees) of every node is in {-1, 0, +1}. Named after Adelson-Velsky and Landis (1962), it was the first self-balancing BST.

avl-delete-may-cascade.text: AVL deletion may require O(log n) rotations because a rotation during delete can decrease the subtree height, propagating imbalance upward (unlike insert where rotation restores height)

avl-delete-retrace.text: AVL delete retracing has OPPOSITE stopping conditions from insert: BF becomes +/-1 -> stop (height unchanged). BF becomes 0 -> continue (height decreased). BF becomes +/-2 -> rotate, may continue if sibling BF != 0.

avl-guaranteed-logarithmic.text: AVL trees provide guaranteed O(log n) worst-case operations because the balance factor invariant (|BF| ≤ 1) prevents degeneration, unlike plain BSTs where sorted insertion creates a linked list.

justifications.label: AVL's balance invariant eliminates the BST degeneration pathology

avl-height-bound.text: AVL tree height h with n nodes: log2(n+1) <= h < log_phi(n+2) + b, where phi = golden ratio ~1.618. Approximately h <= 1.44 * log2(n). Minimum nodes at height h is F(h+2)-1 (Fibonacci).

avl-insert-max-one-rotation.text: AVL insertion requires at most one rotation (single or double) to rebalance because insertion increases subtree height by at most 1, and a single rotation restores the original height

avl-insert-retrace.text: AVL insert retracing: BF becomes 0 -> stop (height unchanged). BF becomes +/-1 -> continue (height increased). BF becomes +/-2 -> rotate then stop (height restored). Retracing is O(1) amortized.

avl-join-split.text: AVL trees support Join and Split operations enabling efficient set operations (union, intersection, difference) in O(m log(n/m + 1)) time. Join requires at most 2 rotations. Split costs O(log n). These operations are parallelizable with depth O(log m * log n).

avl-rotation-asymmetry-explained.text: AVL trees exhibit a fundamental insert/delete asymmetry: insertion needs at most 1 rotation because it increases height by at most 1 (a single rotation absorbs the imbalance), while deletion can cascade O(log n) rotations because a rotation during delete can decrease subtree height, propagating imbalance upward through the tree.

justifications.label: the structural reason for AVL's insert-vs-delete rotation count difference

avl-rotations.text: AVL rebalancing uses 4 rotation cases: Right-Right (single left rotation), Left-Left (single right rotation), Right-Left (double rotation), Left-Right (double rotation). Each rotation is O(1). Insert needs at most 1 rotation; delete may need O(log n) rotations.

avl-tightness-explains-workload-split.text: AVL's tighter balance invariant simultaneously explains its lookup advantage AND its modification cost: the same |BF| ≤ 1 constraint that keeps height within 1.44 log n (faster lookups than red-black's 2 log n) is what forces O(log n) cascading rotations on deletion — this mechanistic link is why AVL favors read-heavy workloads while red-black trees favor write-heavy workloads.

justifications.label: rotation asymmetry (d3) provides the mechanism; family comparison (d2) states the workload preference — combining them reveals the causal link between balance tightness and workload affinity

avl-traversal.text: AVL tree traversal is O(n). After finding a node, next/previous in-order node is accessible in amortized O(1) time, since traversal visits each of (n-1) links exactly twice.

avl-vs-redblack.text: AVL trees are more strictly balanced than red-black trees, making AVL faster for lookup-heavy workloads. Red-black trees need fewer rotations on insert/delete (better for modification-heavy workloads). Both are height-balanced but neither is weight-balanced.

b-plus-tree-leaves-only.text: B+ trees store data only in leaf nodes (internal nodes store only keys for routing), making them efficient for range queries. B* trees delay node splits for higher occupancy. Both are B-tree variants optimized for disk-based storage.

backtracking-complete-parameterized-fram.text: Backtracking is a complete, sound, parameterized search framework: its six-procedure interface (root, reject, accept, first, next, output) provides the systematic enumeration structure that guarantees all valid solutions are found and only valid solutions are reported for finite problems — completeness and soundness are consequences of the framework's parameterized design, not accidental properties.

justifications.label: Completeness/soundness guarantees follow from the six-procedure parameterization structure

backtracking-completeness.text: Backtracking is complete (guaranteed to find all solutions) and sound (only reports valid solutions) for finite problems, unlike many metaheuristics.

backtracking-csp-worst-case.text: For constraint satisfaction problems with n variables each taking m values, backtracking worst case explores the full search tree in O(m^n) time, but pruning typically makes it much faster in practice.

backtracking-definition.text: Backtracking incrementally builds candidate solutions and abandons any candidate as soon as it determines that candidate cannot be completed to a valid solution; it traverses the implicit search tree in depth-first order with pruning.

backtracking-dfs-on-solution-tree.text: Backtracking is structurally a depth-first search over the implicit solution tree: it explores candidate extensions depth-first and prunes entire subtrees via the reject function, mirroring how DFS explores graph branches before backtracking.

justifications.label: both algorithms use the same stack-based exploration-then-backtrack pattern

backtracking-early-pruning.text: Backtracking efficiency depends on the reject function returning true as close to the root as possible, since early pruning eliminates the largest subtrees.

backtracking-pruning-determines-tractabi.text: Backtracking's practical performance on constraint satisfaction problems is strongly influenced by pruning effectiveness: backtracking performs a depth-first search over the implicit solution tree, and the gap between the O(m^n) worst case (every leaf visited) and typical runtime depends on how early the reject function prunes — near-root rejection eliminates entire subtrees, making constraint tightness a major factor in practical runtime alongside problem size.

justifications.label: DFS structure (d1) provides the tree model; early pruning and CSP worst case together show that pruning depth, not problem dimensions, governs practical performance

backtracking-reject-correctness.text: The backtracking reject function must return true ONLY when certain no extension of the candidate can succeed; a false positive causes missed solutions, while a false negative merely reduces efficiency.

backtracking-six-procedures.text: Generic backtracking is defined by six procedural parameters: root(P), reject(P,c), accept(P,c), first(P,c), next(P,s), and output(P,c).

backtracking-universally-tractable.text: Backtracking's complete and sound parameterized framework, combined with early pruning that eliminates entire subtrees near the root, makes it universally tractable for constraint satisfaction problems — the reject function's ability to prune renders the exponential search space manageable.

justifications.label: The m^n worst case (all values for all variables) shows pruning cannot be guaranteed effective — tractability is input-dependent

backtracking-vs-bruteforce.text: Backtracking with a reject function that always returns false degenerates to brute-force enumeration; pruning via the reject function is what distinguishes backtracking from brute force.

balance-design-enables-memory-completene.text: The balanced tree family's coverage of the entire memory hierarchy — from L1 cache (AVL/red-black spectrum) to disk (B-tree/B+/B* family) — can be understood through a two-dimensional design space analogous to hashing's: one axis captures the structural mechanism (reactive rotations for in-memory trees vs. constructive splits for high-fanout disk-friendly trees), while a second axis captures strictness tuning (tight AVL balance vs. relaxed red-black for in-memory; progressive fill guarantees across B-tree variants for disk). This framing suggests that the design space's dimensionality is a useful lens for understanding why balanced trees span the memory hierarchy, though the antecedents do not establish that this dimensionality is the sole or generative cause of that coverage.

justifications.label: 2D design space dimensionality matches memory hierarchy dimensionality enabling complete coverage

balance-design-instantiates-fine-grained.text: The two-dimensional balance design space (mechanism × strictness) is the concrete instantiation of the fine-grained component of hardware awareness: it is precisely through balance tunability that tree data structures adapt from L1 cache (tight AVL) through main memory (relaxed red-black) to disk (wide B-tree), directly realizing data-structure-level hardware codesign.

justifications.label: Balance tunability is the mechanism through which fine-grained hardware awareness is achieved

balance-design-two-dimensional-space.text: Tree balance design is a two-dimensional optimization space: the mechanism dimension (reactive rotation in AVL/red-black vs. constructive splitting in B-trees) determines rebalancing cost and code complexity, while the strictness dimension (tight AVL → relaxed red-black → broad B-tree) adapts to the memory hierarchy — and the dimensions interact, since constructive mechanisms naturally admit the wider branching factors needed for disk optimization.

justifications.label: Mechanism choice and strictness level jointly determine tree suitability for a hardware tier

balance-mechanism-duality.text: AVL trees and B-trees illustrate two contrasting approaches to maintaining balance in tree data structures: AVL trees use reactive correction, detecting imbalance after mutations and repairing via rotations with a characteristic insert/delete asymmetry (at most 1 rotation for insertion vs O(log n) for deletion, since deletion-triggered rotations can decrease subtree height and propagate imbalance upward); B-trees use proactive structural enforcement, maintaining balance as a construction invariant through minimum fill guarantees (⌈m/2⌉ children per non-root node), overflow splits that propagate median keys upward, and depth changes that occur exclusively through root operations, without requiring rotations.

justifications.label: B-tree balance-by-construction (depth-1) and AVL rotation asymmetry (depth-3) represent the two poles of the balance mechanism design space

balance-strictness-adapts-to-memory-tier.text: Balance strictness is a design parameter that varies across tree structures suited to different storage tiers: AVL's tight |BF|≤1 constraint simultaneously explains its lookup advantage and modification cost, red-black trees relax balance to reduce rotations while serving as a structural bridge between binary and multi-way trees, and B-trees maximize branching factor to reduce disk I/O — suggesting a common balance-vs-modification tradeoff that adapts to different access cost characteristics.

justifications.label: Depth-5 synthesis connecting AVL's balance-strictness tradeoff to the full memory-hierarchy spectrum

balance-strictness-realizes-hardware-cod.text: Balance strictness is the specific tunable parameter by which tree data structures achieve hardware codesign: the same abstract balanced BST concept manifests as AVL (tight |BF|≤1 for L1/L2 cache lookup speed), red-black (relaxed balance for modification-heavy RAM workloads), and B-tree (maximally wide branching for disk I/O minimization), and this parameter tuning at the data structure level composes with divide-and-conquer's cache-obliviousness at the algorithm level to produce hardware-aware computation spanning the entire memory hierarchy.

justifications.label: Balance strictness (d5) is the concrete mechanism implementing hardware codesign (d6) — it makes the abstract hardware-awareness principle actionable through a single tunable parameter.

balanced-bst-family-unified.text: AVL trees and red-black trees are both self-balancing BSTs with O(log n) operations but different balance strictness: AVL maintains tighter balance (height ratio < 1.44 log n) favoring lookups, while red-black allows looser balance (height ≤ 2 log n) favoring modifications — and red-black's invariants are actually B-tree constraints in binary form.

justifications.label: two BST balancing strategies unified as points on a strictness-vs-modification-cost spectrum

balanced-bst-memory-hierarchy-spectrum.text: Balanced search trees exhibit a spectrum of balance strictness and branching factor adapted to different access patterns: AVL trees maintain tighter balance (height < 1.44 log n), favoring lookups; red-black trees allow looser balance (height ≤ 2 log n), favoring modifications, with invariants that correspond to B-tree constraints in binary form; and B-trees use multi-way branching to reduce disk I/O from O(log₂ N) to O(log_b N), making them the standard index structure in databases and file systems. Red-black trees thus serve as a structural bridge between binary in-memory trees and multi-way external-memory trees.

justifications.label: BST family comparison (d2) covers the AVL/red-black in-memory spectrum; B-tree disk advantage covers the external-memory endpoint — red-black's 2-3-4 isomorphism bridges the two

balanced-trees-complete-memory-hierarchy.text: The balanced tree family provides a complete storage solution spanning the entire memory hierarchy from L1 cache to spinning disk: in-memory access is covered by the AVL/red-black balance strictness spectrum (tight AVL for lookup-heavy, relaxed red-black for modification-heavy workloads), while disk and external storage is covered by the B-tree/B+/B* progressive optimization family (increasing minimum fill and leaf-only data storage reduce I/O from O(log_2 N) to O(log_b N)).

justifications.label: In-memory balance spectrum (AVL/red-black) and disk optimization family (B-tree variants) together cover every memory tier

bellman-equation-unifies-shortest-path-d.text: The Bellman equation V(s) = opt{cost + V(next)} is the common theoretical foundation of both Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall: Bellman-Ford decomposes by path length (single-source), Floyd-Warshall decomposes by intermediate vertices (all-pairs) — both are DP over the same recurrence.

justifications.label: two shortest-path algorithms as different DP decompositions of the same equation

bellman-ford-complete-negative-weight-so.text: Bellman-Ford is the complete single-source solution for negative-weight graphs: iterative relaxation computes shortest paths, and one additional pass detects negative cycles that make shortest paths undefined.

justifications.label: depth-2 — two derived capabilities combine into a complete negative-weight toolkit

bellman-ford-definition.text: The Bellman-Ford algorithm computes single-source shortest paths in weighted directed graphs, including those with negative edge weights. Time: O(|V|·|E|), Space: O(|V|).

bellman-ford-dijkstra-complementary-cove.text: Bellman-Ford and Dijkstra partition the single-source shortest path problem by edge weight sign: Dijkstra is faster (O(|E| + |V| log |V|) with Fibonacci heap) but requires non-negative weights, while Bellman-Ford is slower (O(|V||E|)) but handles negative weights and detects negative cycles — together they cover all cases.

justifications.label: Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford complement each other across the negative-weight boundary

bellman-ford-early-termination.text: Early termination optimization: if an iteration of Bellman-Ford relaxes no edges, the algorithm can stop immediately — all shortest paths are found and no negative cycles exist. Reduces best-case complexity from O(|V|·|E|) to O(|E|).

bellman-ford-improvements.text: Yen (1970) reduces Bellman-Ford worst-case iterations from |V|-1 to |V|/2 by partitioning edges into forward/backward sets. Bannister-Eppstein (2012) uses random vertex ordering to reduce expected iterations to |V|/3. Fineman (2024) achieves O~(|V|^{8/9}·|E|) with high probability.

metadata.repair_research: The specific published results (Yen 1970, Bannister-Eppstein 2012, Fineman 2024) are factual claims about academic papers that cannot be derived from the basic Bellman-Ford definition alone. They are plausible and worth preserving, but need verification against the actual Wikipedia source to confirm the exact bounds and years. Rather than abandoning valuable improvement history or softening already-specific claims, the right move is to verify these facts against the source material and then re-justify the belief as a premise sourced from Wikipedia, not as a derivation from the base definition.

bellman-ford-negative-cycles.text: Bellman-Ford detects negative cycles: after |V|-1 iterations, a final pass checks if any edge can still be relaxed. If so, a negative cycle is reachable from the source. The relaxable edge may not be on the cycle itself — must trace predecessors to find the actual cycle.

bellman-ford-optimization-synergy.text: SPFA and early termination are complementary Bellman-Ford optimizations operating at different granularities: SPFA reduces per-iteration work by only relaxing from changed vertices, while early termination eliminates entire iterations when no edges are relaxed.

justifications.label: depth-3 — combines two independent optimization strategies at different levels of the algorithm

bellman-ford-relaxation.text: Bellman-Ford works by relaxation: it relaxes ALL edges |V|-1 times. After i iterations, distance[v] equals the shortest path from source to v using at most i edges. The |V|-1 bound follows from the maximum simple path length.

bellman-ford-routing.text: Distributed Bellman-Ford is the basis of distance-vector routing protocols (e.g., RIP). Each node shares its distance table with neighbors. Disadvantages: poor scalability, slow topology convergence, count-to-infinity problem.

metadata.repair_research: The claim about distributed Bellman-Ford being the basis of distance-vector routing (RIP), neighbor distance-table sharing, and the count-to-infinity problem are all factually correct and well-established. However, these are application-domain facts about networking protocols that cannot be derived solely from the algorithm's mathematical definition. Since the source domain is Wikipedia, a Wikipedia article on distance-vector routing or RIP would provide the missing antecedent to ground these claims. Rather than softening (the claims are accurate, not overstated) or abandoning (the belief is valuable and correct), research to find or create the missing networking-domain premise is the right path.

bellman-ford-spfa.text: The Shortest Path Faster Algorithm (SPFA) is Moore's 1959 variant of Bellman-Ford that maintains a queue of vertices whose outgoing edges need relaxation, avoiding redundant relaxations. Constant-factor improvement for dense graphs; same O(|V|·|E|) worst case.

metadata.repair_research: The claim that SPFA is Moore's 1959 queue-based variant with specific performance characteristics is a historical and algorithmic fact that cannot be derived from the basic Bellman-Ford definition alone. It's a plausible and likely correct claim, but confirming the historical attribution (Moore 1959) and the precise characterization requires consulting the Wikipedia source. Rather than abandoning a likely-valid belief or softening it unnecessarily, it should be researched against the source material to either confirm and properly justify it, or correct any inaccuracies.

bellman-ford-theory-practice-complete.text: Bellman-Ford is simultaneously theoretically complete (handles negative weights, detects negative cycles via an additional relaxation pass) and practically optimizable (SPFA reduces per-iteration work via queue-based selective relaxation, early termination eliminates unnecessary iterations when convergence is reached) — a rare combination where full generality coexists with meaningful constant-factor improvements on typical inputs.

justifications.label: Full negative-weight generality AND practical optimizations in the same algorithm

bellman-ford-vs-dijkstra.text: Bellman-Ford handles negative edge weights but is slower than Dijkstra. Dijkstra greedily selects the closest unprocessed vertex via a priority queue; Bellman-Ford simply relaxes all edges each iteration. Dijkstra fails with negative weights because it assumes processed vertices have final distances.

bfs-complexity.text: BFS has time complexity O(|V|+|E|) for explicit graphs and space complexity O(|V|); for implicit graphs with branching factor b and depth d, time is O(b^(d+1))

bfs-definition.text: Breadth-first search is a queue-based graph traversal algorithm that explores all vertices at the current depth before moving to the next level (level-order traversal)

bfs-dfs-complementary-across-all-axes.text: BFS and DFS are complementary across every analysis dimension: frontier structure (queue vs stack), optimality property (shortest unweighted paths vs structural decomposition), and space complexity (O(width) vs O(height)) — making them jointly exhaustive as the two fundamental graph traversal strategies, with tree shape determining which is space-efficient for a given problem.

justifications.label: Complementarity extends beyond data structure choice to optimality and space, with tree shape as the arbiter

bfs-dfs-dual-traversal.text: BFS and DFS are graph traversals whose fundamental distinction is the frontier data structure: BFS uses a queue (exploring level by level, finding shortest paths in unweighted graphs), DFS uses a stack (exploring depth-first before backtracking). DFS does not guarantee shortest paths. Both follow a similar traversal skeleton with different exploration orders.

justifications.label: BFS and DFS are the same algorithm with queue vs stack, yielding complementary guarantees

bfs-queue-dfs-stack.text: Breadth-first search uses a queue to explore graph nodes level by level; depth-first search uses a stack. The choice of data structure is the fundamental distinction between the two traversal strategies.

bfs-shortest-path-unweighted.text: BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs and is complete (guaranteed to find a solution if one exists); it is optimal for unweighted shortest paths

big-o-domain-matters.text: The same function can have different Big O characterizations on finite vs. infinite domains; Taylor approximation uses finite-domain Big O while algorithm analysis uses infinite-domain Big O.

big-o-formal-definition.text: f(x) = O(g(x)) means there exists a positive constant M such that |f(x)| ≤ M·g(x) for all x in the domain; the implied constant M must exist but its specific value does not matter.

big-o-not-equality.text: The '=' in f(x) = O(g(x)) denotes set membership, not equality; it is not symmetric — writing O(g(x)) = f(x) is invalid.

big-o-simplification.text: In Big O notation (as x → ∞), constant factors and lower-order terms are dropped: in a sum keep only the term with the largest growth rate; in a product drop factors not depending on the variable.

big-o-tightness.text: A Big O bound can be technically correct but not tight: O(x^10) is valid for a degree-4 polynomial but uselessly loose; the tightest correct bound should be preferred.

big-o-upper-bound-only.text: Big O provides an asymptotic upper bound only and says nothing about lower bounds; Θ (Theta) notation gives a tight bound covering both upper and lower bounds.

binary-heap-array-formulas.text: A binary heap is stored implicitly in an array with no pointer overhead. With 0-based indexing: left child = 2i+1, right child = 2i+2, parent = floor((i-1)/2). With 1-based indexing: left child = 2i, right child = 2i+1, parent = floor(i/2).

binary-heap-operations-complexity.text: Binary heap operation complexities: find-max Θ(1), insert Θ(log n), extract-max Θ(log n), increase-key Θ(log n), merge Θ(n). Insert uses sift-up; extract-max replaces root with last element then sift-down.

binary-search-analytical-and-practical-p.text: Binary search occupies a uniquely dual position in the algorithms canon: it is the analytical exemplar (tight worst-case bound of floor(log₂ n)+1 comparisons plus dual correctness requirements demonstrating dual-axis rigor) and simultaneously the practical terminal of the sorting pipeline (sorting's O(n log n) satisfiability makes O(log n) lookup universally applicable), connecting the canon's theoretical analytical framework to its practical computational pipeline at a single algorithm.

justifications.label: Binary search is simultaneously the analytical exemplar of dual-axis rigor and the practical terminal of the sorting pipeline

binary-search-definition.text: Binary search finds a target value in a sorted array by repeatedly halving the search interval; it runs in O(log n) worst/average case, O(1) best case, with O(1) space, and is optimal among comparison-based searches on sorted arrays.

binary-search-dual-correctness-requireme.text: Binary search has two independent correctness requirements operating at different levels: the algorithmic precondition that input must be sorted (violating it produces silently wrong results), and the implementation precondition that midpoint calculation must use L + floor((R-L)/2) rather than (L+R)/2 to avoid integer overflow (a bug that went undetected in standard libraries for decades). Both failures are silent — no error, just wrong answers.

justifications.label: Two independent failure modes that share the dangerous property of producing wrong results silently

binary-search-exemplifies-dual-axis-rigo.text: Binary search is the canonical exemplar of the canon's dual-axis analytical rigor: its tight worst-case bound (floor(log₂ n) + 1 comparisons) satisfies the performance axis with exact precision, while its dual correctness requirements (sorted precondition + overflow-safe midpoint) satisfy the correctness axis at two independent levels, making it the most completely analyzed single algorithm in the canon.

justifications.label: Binary search simultaneously exhibits tight performance bounds and multi-level correctness analysis

binary-search-exhaustively-analyzed.text: Binary search is one of the most exhaustively analyzed algorithms in the canon: its performance is exactly characterized (floor(log₂ n) + 1 worst-case comparisons, not merely O(log n)), its leftmost variant enables rank queries beyond simple membership, and its correctness has two independent failure modes (unsorted input violating the precondition, integer overflow in the midpoint calculation) — yet implementations remain error-prone despite this thorough understanding.

justifications.label: Precise performance bounds, variant semantics, and dual correctness pitfalls make binary search uniquely well-characterized

binary-search-leftmost-variant.text: The leftmost binary search variant initializes R = n (not n-1) and returns the rank of T (count of elements less than T) even when T is absent from the array.

binary-search-operationalizes-ordering.text: Binary search is the canonical mechanism that converts the ordering invariant into computational power: the universal ordering principle is merely structural without a mechanism to exploit it, and binary search's O(log n) lookup is precisely that exploitation — its dual position as both the analytical exemplar (tight worst-case bound) and the universally applicable tool (any sortable dataset) demonstrates it as the primary bridge from ordering invariant to efficient computation.

justifications.label: Binary search's dual analytical/practical role (depth-6) is explained by its function as the operationalizer of the universal ordering invariant (depth-7)

binary-search-overflow-bug.text: The midpoint calculation (L + R) / 2 can cause integer overflow; the correct form is L + floor((R - L) / 2).

binary-search-precisely-characterized.text: Binary search is precisely characterized beyond its O(log n) asymptotic bound: it requires exactly floor(log2 n) + 1 worst-case comparisons (a tight count, not merely an order), and the leftmost variant extends the basic algorithm to compute rank (count of elements less than the target), demonstrating that the simple binary search template supports exact analysis and variant specialization.

justifications.label: Two orphaned binary search beliefs combine to show precise characterization beyond asymptotics

binary-search-precondition-sorted.text: Binary search requires the input array to be sorted as a precondition; it cannot be applied to unsorted arrays.

binary-search-universal-ordered-access-p.text: Binary search is the canon's universal ordered access primitive: it operationalizes ordering into computational power (converting the universal invariant to O(log n) access), is universally applicable (the sorting precondition is always satisfiable), and its tight worst-case characterization makes it the analytical exemplar of the canon's dual-axis rigor — achieving simultaneous universality in applicability, performance analysis, and ordering activation.

justifications.label: Ordering operationalization (depth-8) + dual-axis analytical exemplar (depth-6) = universal primitive, gated by the overflow implementation pitfall

binary-search-universally-applicable.text: Binary search's O(log n) lookup can be applied to any sortable dataset because the sorting precondition is satisfiable at O(n log n) or better cost — the comprehensively resolved sorting landscape (introsort, timsort, and radix sort covering all practical regimes) means that preprocessing for binary search is typically not the bottleneck.

justifications.label: Sorting being fully resolved removes binary search's only precondition as a practical barrier

binary-search-vs-hash-table.text: Hash tables provide O(1) average lookup (faster than binary search's O(log n)), but cannot support ordered queries such as rank, predecessor, successor, or range queries.

binary-search-worst-comparisons.text: Binary search requires exactly floor(log2 n) + 1 comparisons in the worst case.

binary-tree-array-indexing.text: In array storage of a complete binary tree (0-indexed), left child is at 2i+1, right child at 2i+2, parent at floor((i-1)/2); 1-indexed: left=2i, right=2i+1, parent=floor(i/2)

binary-tree-catalan-count.text: The number of structurally distinct full binary trees with n internal nodes equals the nth Catalan number C_n

binary-tree-complete-definition.text: A complete binary tree has every level completely filled except possibly the last, where nodes are packed as far left as possible; it can be efficiently stored in an array with zero wasted space

binary-tree-definition.text: A binary tree is a tree data structure in which each node has at most two children (left and right); it is a k-ary tree with k = 2

binary-tree-degenerate.text: A degenerate (pathological) binary tree has each parent with only one child, making it structurally equivalent to a linked list with O(n) search instead of O(log n)

binary-tree-duality-grounds-inter-pillar.text: The binary tree's dual organizing paradigms (heap-ordered for O(1) priority access, search-ordered for O(log n) sorted access) are the concrete substrate-level mechanism enabling the canon's double inter-pillar connection: heap-ordered trees implement the priority queues that power the sorting→Dijkstra/Prim pipeline connecting sorting to graph optimization, while search-ordered trees implement the BSTs powering ordered computation — making the tree's internal structural bifurcation the physical realization of the canon's two-pillar architecture.

justifications.label: Binary tree duality (depth 2, concrete property) explains inter-pillar double connection (depth 8, abstract structure) at the substrate level — the tree is the atom from which pillar linkage is built

binary-tree-edges.text: A binary tree with n nodes has exactly n - 1 edges, since every node except the root has exactly one incoming edge

binary-tree-full-definition.text: A full (proper/strict/plane) binary tree is one where every node has either 0 or 2 children — no node has exactly one child

binary-tree-hardware-aware-operational-n.text: The binary tree serves as a primary hardware-aware operational nexus in the canon: it operationalizes the dual universal mechanisms (ordering and traversal) into concrete computational power on a single structure, while the canon's complete hardware story spans from cache optimization (pervading all abstraction levels) through hardware codesign (operating at multiple granularities) — making the binary tree a key structure where operational universality and hardware awareness intersect.

justifications.label: Binary trees are where the canon's operational universality meets its full-vertical hardware awareness

binary-tree-leaves-eq-degree2-plus1.text: In any non-empty binary tree, the number of leaves equals the number of degree-2 (internal with two children) nodes plus 1: l = i₂ + 1

binary-tree-nexus-operationalizes-dual-m.text: The binary tree's dual bridging roles (structural inter-pillar connection via heap/search ordering, physical hardware bridge via balance design) are the concrete implementation locus where the canon's two universal operational mechanisms — ordering (the invariant) and traversal (the activation) — become simultaneously exercisable on a single data structure.

justifications.label: Binary tree as dual bridge (depth-10) is where ordering and traversal duality (depth-8) converge in a single implementation substrate

binary-tree-null-links.text: A binary tree with n nodes contains exactly n + 1 null links (null child pointers)

binary-tree-perfect-definition.text: A perfect binary tree has all interior nodes with exactly two children and all leaves at the same depth; it has 2^h leaves and 2^(h+1) - 1 total nodes at height h

binary-tree-quantitative-and-combinatori.text: Binary trees admit exhaustive quantitative characterization at two complementary levels: structural counting laws (n−1 edges, n+1 null links, leaves = degree-2 nodes + 1) describe fixed relationships within any single tree, while the Catalan number formula (C_n distinct structures with n internal nodes) counts the space of all possible trees — together providing both internal structure constraints and external enumeration of the design space.

justifications.label: Internal counting laws and Catalan enumeration exhaustively characterize binary tree structure

binary-tree-structural-and-physical-brid.text: The binary tree is the canon's central implementation nexus serving dual bridging roles: structurally, its dual organizing paradigms (heap-ordered for O(1) priority access, search-ordered for O(log n) sorted access) ground the inter-pillar connection between graph optimization and sorting/computation; physically, its balance design space (reactive rotation vs. constructive splitting, tight AVL to loose B-tree) instantiates fine-grained hardware awareness across memory tiers — making the binary tree simultaneously the bridge between content domains and the bridge between memory levels.

justifications.label: Dual paradigms ground inter-pillar bridge + balance design grounds hardware bridge = dual-bridge nexus

binary-tree-structural-counting-laws.text: Binary trees satisfy three complementary counting invariants derivable from the fixed branching factor of 2: exactly n−1 edges (one incoming per non-root node), exactly n+1 null links (2n child pointers minus n−1 used edges), and leaves = degree-2 nodes + 1 — enabling O(1) structural metric computation without traversal.

justifications.label: three counting properties arise from the branching-factor-2 constraint

binary-tree-supports-dual-organizing-par.text: Binary trees' structural counting invariants (n-1 edges, n+1 null links, leaves = degree-2 nodes + 1) characterize a shared structure upon which two contrasting organizing paradigms operate: the heap property (parent dominates children, enabling O(1) priority access but sacrificing arbitrary search) and the BST property (left < node < right, enabling O(log n) ordered search but requiring O(log n) priority access) — with the choice between them determined by whether the workload is priority-dominated or search-dominated.

justifications.label: Binary tree counting laws underpin both heap and BST organizing principles from one structural foundation

binary-tree-universal-ordered-substrate.text: Binary trees provide a versatile foundation for ordered computation: their dual organizing paradigms (heap-ordered for O(1) priority access, search-ordered for O(log n) sorted retrieval) combined with the AVL/red-black balance-strictness spectrum address a wide range of ordered data access patterns — from priority queues through lookup-heavy retrieval to write-heavy sorted containers.

justifications.label: Heap/BST duality plus balance-strictness spectrum yields complete ordered access coverage

block-sort-resolves-stable-inplace-trile.text: Block sort uniquely resolves the comparison-sort trilemma by achieving all three desirable properties simultaneously: O(n log n) worst-case time, stability, and O(1) extra space — the only known algorithm to do so, demonstrating that the trilemma (where merge sort sacrifices space, heapsort sacrifices stability, and quicksort sacrifices worst-case time) is not a fundamental impossibility but an artifact of the specific algorithms in the standard repertoire.

justifications.label: The trilemma establishes that the three standard sorts each sacrifice one property; block sort's existence as the sole algorithm achieving all three reveals the trilemma is a practical constraint of common algorithms, not a theoretical barrier.

block-sort-unique.text: Block sort is the only known O(n log n) comparison sort that is both stable and uses only O(1) extra memory.

bloom-extends-hashing-to-probabilistic-r.text: Bloom filters occupy one end of the precision axis within hashing's two-dimensional design space (collision strategy × precision spectrum): where hash tables operate in the exact-answer regime choosing between chaining and open addressing, Bloom filters trade exactness for space efficiency — accepting tunable false positives with zero false negatives — extending hashing from deterministic lookup to probabilistic membership testing within the same design framework

justifications.label: Bloom filters add a probabilistic axis to the hashing design space

bloom-filter-properties.text: A Bloom filter is a probabilistic data structure with no false negatives, tunable false positive rate, and space-efficient membership testing. Standard Bloom filters cannot support deletion; counting variants can.

bplus-tree-variant.text: A B+ tree stores all record pointers only in leaf nodes and links leaves for fast sequential access; internal nodes hold more keys (no record pointers), making the tree shallower than a standard B-tree.

brodal-queue-optimal-bounds.text: Brodal queues and strict Fibonacci heaps achieve theoretically optimal worst-case (not amortized) bounds: Θ(1) for find-max, insert, increase-key, and meld; Θ(log n) for delete-max.

bst-definition.text: A binary search tree (BST) is a rooted binary tree where each node's key is greater than all keys in its left subtree and less than all keys in its right subtree, enabling O(log n) average-case search, insert, and delete.

bst-deletion-reduces-to-successor.text: BST deletion's most complex case (node with two children) reduces to the in-order successor algorithm: replace the node's key with its successor (minimum of right subtree), then delete the successor node which has at most one child — decomposing the three-case deletion problem into successor lookup plus the simpler one-child case.

justifications.label: Two-children deletion decomposes into successor finding plus one-child deletion

bst-deletion-three-cases.text: BST deletion has three cases: leaf node (replace with NIL), one child (elevate the child), two children (replace with in-order successor or predecessor).

bst-inorder-sorted.text: Inorder traversal (left, node, right) of a BST yields keys in sorted order; this is the defining operational characteristic of the BST property.

bst-insert-always-leaf.text: In a standard BST, new nodes are always inserted as leaves by descending like search using a trailing pointer and attaching at the NIL position.

bst-logarithmic-guarantee.text: A BST provides O(log n) search, insert, and delete operations with in-order traversal yielding sorted output.

justifications.label: logarithmic performance holds only when the tree is prevented from degenerating to a linked list

bst-operations-reduce-to-ordering.text: BST operations are unified by their common reduction to the in-order relationship: search descends by comparing against the BST ordering invariant, deletion's most complex case reduces to finding the in-order successor, and traversal in-order yields sorted output — all three core operations are manifestations of the same ordering structure that defines the BST.

justifications.label: Search, deletion, and traversal all reduce to the BST ordering invariant

bst-successor-algorithm.text: The in-order successor of node x in a BST is the minimum of x's right subtree if it exists; otherwise, walk up ancestors until finding the first ancestor where x is in the left subtree.

bst-worst-case-degenerate.text: Without balancing, a BST degenerates to a linked list with O(n) worst-case operations; sorted insertion is the classic degeneracy scenario producing tree height n.

bstar-tree-variant.text: A B* tree requires nodes to be at least 2/3 full (vs B-tree's 1/2) and delays splits by redistributing keys to siblings first.

btree-balance-by-construction.text: B-tree balance is maintained by a three-part structural mechanism rather than explicit rotations: minimum fill guarantees (⌈m/2⌉ children per non-root node) prevent under-utilization, overflow splits propagate median keys upward, and depth changes occur exclusively through root operations — ensuring all leaves remain at the same depth as a construction invariant.

justifications.label: split + fill + root-only depth change = balance without rotations

btree-complexity.text: B-tree search, insert, and delete are all O(log n) in both amortized and worst case; space complexity is O(n).

btree-definition.text: A B-tree is a self-balancing tree data structure where all leaves are at the same depth, invented by Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight in 1970 at Boeing Research Labs.

btree-depth-change-rules.text: B-tree depth increases only when the root splits; depth decreases only when the root's two children merge — depth changes are global events, not local.

btree-disk-io-advantage.text: B-trees reduce disk reads from O(log₂ N) (binary tree) to O(log_b N) where b is the blocking factor (keys per node), making them the standard index structure in virtually all relational databases and file systems.

btree-family-spans-disk-optimization.text: The B-tree family forms a progressive optimization spectrum for disk-based storage: standard B-trees reduce I/O from O(log_2 N) to O(log_b N), B+ trees further optimize range queries by storing data only in linked leaves, and B* trees maximize node utilization by requiring 2/3 fill and redistributing before splitting — each variant sacrifices simplicity for a specific I/O or space improvement.

justifications.label: Three B-tree variants form a specialization chain, each targeting a different disk storage optimization

btree-height-formulas.text: B-tree height bounds: minimum h = ⌈log_m(n+1)⌉ − 1; maximum h = ⌊log_d((n+1)/2)⌋ where d = ⌈m/2⌉.

btree-minimum-fill.text: Every non-root internal node in a B-tree of order m has at least ⌈m/2⌉ children (at least half full).

btree-order-knuth.text: Under Knuth's definition, a B-tree of order m allows each node at most m children and m−1 keys; the 'order' definition is ambiguous in the literature (Knuth = max children, others = min keys).

btree-split-on-overflow.text: Inserting into a full B-tree node (2d keys) splits it into two d-key siblings, pushing the median key up to the parent; if the root splits, a new root is created and the tree grows taller by 1.

bucket-sort-average-case.text: Bucket sort achieves O(n) average-case time when the number of buckets k = Theta(n) and input is uniformly distributed; the exact average is O(n + n²/k + k)

bucket-sort-counting-sort-degenerate.text: Bucket sort with bucket size 1 degenerates to counting sort; bucket sort trades counting sort's O(n + M) worst-case guarantee for lower O(n) average-case memory

bucket-sort-definition.text: Bucket sort is a distribution sort that scatters elements into k buckets based on value, sorts each bucket individually (typically with insertion sort), then concatenates the results

bucket-sort-space.text: Bucket sort has space complexity O(n + k) where n is the number of elements and k is the number of buckets

bucket-sort-two-buckets-quicksort.text: Bucket sort with 2 buckets is effectively quicksort with the pivot at the midpoint of the value range

bucket-sort-worst-case.text: Bucket sort worst case is O(n²) when all elements cluster into one bucket (using insertion sort per bucket); worst case becomes O(n log n) if merge sort is used per bucket instead

cache-friendly-implicit-array-trees.text: Binary heaps and Fenwick trees both use implicit array storage with arithmetic indexing to navigate tree structure without pointers — heaps via 2i+1/2i+2 formulas, Fenwick trees via the bit manipulation i & (-i). This arithmetic approach avoids pointer-chasing overhead.

justifications.label: two different implicit-tree-in-array encodings using different arithmetic schemes

cache-hardware-complete-vertical-story.text: Cache performance optimization and hardware codesign together constitute the canon's complete hardware story along its full vertical extent: cache optimization pervades all three abstraction levels (data layout, algorithm structure, data structure encoding), while hardware codesign operates at two complementary granularities (fine-grained balance tuning, coarse-grained representation choice) — together they ensure hardware awareness is never merely a single-level concern.

justifications.label: Three-level cache story (depth-6) + two-granularity hardware codesign (depth-10) = complete vertical hardware awareness

cache-performance-dual-level-design.text: Cache performance in algorithms is governed at two independent design levels: at the data level, array memory layout (row-major vs column-major) determines which iteration patterns achieve the optimal ceil(nk/B) cache misses; at the algorithmic level, divide-and-conquer's recursive decomposition naturally becomes cache-oblivious when sub-problems fit in cache, providing both parallelism and locality without explicit cache-size knowledge.

justifications.label: Cache efficiency arises from both data layout choices (row/column-major) and algorithmic structure (DnC recursion)

cache-performance-spans-all-abstraction-.text: Cache performance optimization pervades the algorithms canon at every abstraction level: at the data level, array memory layout governs which iteration patterns achieve optimal cache miss rates; at the algorithm level, divide-and-conquer provides cache-oblivious behavior through recursive decomposition; and at the data structure level, array-implicit trees exploit cache-friendly sequential access — constituting a three-level cache story paralleling the canon's three-layer computational architecture.

justifications.label: Data+algorithm cache design (depth-2) combined with tree-level hardware bridging (depth-5) reveals cache optimization at all three architecture layers

call-stack-dual-role-foundation-and-vuln.text: The call stack serves a paradoxical dual role in computing: it is simultaneously the foundational substrate enabling recursion, DFS, backtracking, and expression evaluation (the algorithmic foundation), and a security vulnerability where sharing data and return addresses on the same stack creates attack surfaces for buffer overflow exploits — the same design that makes it computationally indispensable makes it the primary target for control-flow hijacking.

justifications.label: The stack's computational indispensability and security vulnerability arise from the same shared-memory design

call-stack-security.text: The call stack stores return addresses and local variables; sharing data and return addresses on the same stack creates stack smashing (buffer overflow) vulnerabilities.

canon-2x2-organizational-structure.text: The algorithms canon exhibits a 2x2 organizational structure: two content pillars (graph optimization and sorting/ordered computation) are analyzed by two complementary meta-techniques (DP for optimization strategy and amortized analysis for performance guarantees), with each meta-technique applying across both pillars — DP unifies shortest path and knapsack; amortized analysis validates Fibonacci heaps and dynamic arrays.

justifications.label: Two depth-6 orthogonal decompositions (content pillars and meta-techniques) reveal a 2x2 matrix structure
