hash-table-default-lookup.text: Hash tables are the default O(1) lookup structure for key-value retrieval workloads.

justifications.label: hash tables are preferred only when ordered operations (min, max, range) are not needed

hash-table-load-factor.text: Hash table load factor α = n/m (stored elements / total buckets) is the key metric governing performance; tables are resized when α exceeds a threshold α_max

hash-table-no-ordered-ops.text: Hash tables cannot efficiently support ordered operations (min, max, successor, range queries); balanced BSTs are preferred for workloads requiring sorted-order access

hash-table-rehashing-amortized.text: Hash table rehashing (triggered when α exceeds α_max) doubles the table size and recomputes all hash indices; amortized cost is O(1) per operation over time

hashing-precision-space-extreme-endpoint.text: Perfect hashing and Bloom filters occupy opposite endpoints of the hash precision-space tradeoff: perfect hashing guarantees zero collisions (maximum precision) at the cost of requiring complete key-set knowledge, while Bloom filters accept tunable false positives (minimum precision) to achieve sub-linear space with no key-set constraints — together they bound the full design space between exact and probabilistic membership testing.

justifications.label: Perfect hashing and Bloom filters mark the precision endpoints of hash-based membership testing

hashing-precision-spectrum.text: Hashing-based data structures span a precision spectrum from zero-collision determinism to tunable-error probabilism: perfect hash functions guarantee zero collisions by precomputing an injective mapping over a known key set, while Bloom filters accept tunable false positives in exchange for extreme space efficiency and no key-set preregistration — opposite design points trading precision for flexibility and space.

justifications.label: Two base beliefs describe hashing structures at opposite extremes of the precision/flexibility tradeoff; combining them reveals a spectrum where the fundamental design choice is how much collision tolerance to accept in exchange for space and generality.

hashing-sufficient-for-all-lookup.text: Hashing's two-dimensional internal design space (collision strategy × precision spectrum) provides sufficient coverage for all practical lookup workloads, making hash-based structures the single universal lookup solution without requiring BSTs or tries.

justifications.label: Hashing covers all unordered lookup but cannot support ordered or range queries, necessitating BSTs and tries

hashing-two-dimensional-design-space.text: Hashing-based data structures exhibit at least two independently varying design dimensions: collision resolution strategy (chaining with α > 1 tolerance vs. probing with α < 1 hard limit), which shapes steady-state performance characteristics, and precision guarantee (zero-collision perfect hashing to tunable-error Bloom filters), which governs a correctness-space tradeoff. These axes appear composable, though the antecedents establish them independently rather than demonstrating their full combinatorial interaction.

justifications.label: Collision handling and precision are orthogonal design axes that compose independently

heap-bst-access-pattern-duality.text: Heaps and BSTs represent a fundamental access-pattern duality despite both being binary tree structures: heaps sacrifice arbitrary search (O(n)) to achieve O(1) priority access via the heap property, while BSTs provide O(log n) search via the ordering invariant at the cost of O(log n) priority access — making the choice purely a function of whether the workload is priority-dominated or search-dominated.

justifications.label: The heap property and BST ordering invariant are complementary rather than competing design choices

heap-property-definition.text: A heap satisfies the heap property: in a max-heap every parent key >= its children's keys; in a min-heap every parent key <= its children's keys. Only vertical (parent-child) relationships are constrained — siblings and cousins have no ordering.

heap-replace-operation.text: The heap replace operation (pop root and push new key) is more efficient than separate extract + insert because it requires only one sift-down pass instead of a sift-down followed by a sift-up.

heap-stdlib-implementations.text: Standard library heap implementations: Python heapq (min-heap), Java PriorityQueue (min-heap default), C++ std::priority_queue (max-heap default), Rust BinaryHeap (max-heap), Go container/heap (interface-based), .NET PriorityQueue (.NET 6+, min-heap, quaternary).

heap-vs-bst-no-search.text: Unlike binary search trees, heaps have no sibling ordering and do not support efficient search for arbitrary elements, ordered traversal, or predecessor/successor queries.

heapsort-all-case-nlogn.text: Heapsort has O(n log n) time complexity in best, average, and worst cases for distinct keys. Best case is O(n) when all keys are equal. It uses O(1) auxiliary space (in-place).

heapsort-cache-optimal-inplace-sort.text: Heapsort achieves the ideal combination of theoretical optimality and cache-friendly implementation: O(n log n) worst-case time with O(1) extra space, built on the array-implicit binary heap whose contiguous memory layout and arithmetic navigation eliminate pointer-chasing overhead — the theoretically and practically complete in-place comparison sort.

justifications.label: Heapsort's cache-optimality argument is theoretically sound but gated by empirical evidence of 2-3x slowdown vs quicksort

heapsort-complexity.text: Heapsort runs in O(n log n) in all cases, uses O(1) extra memory (in-place), and is not stable.

heapsort-introsort-fallback.text: Introsort is a hybrid sorting algorithm that starts with quicksort and falls back to heapsort when it detects degenerate O(n²) behavior, guaranteeing O(n log n) worst case. Pattern-defeating quicksort also uses heapsort as a fallback.

heapsort-not-stable.text: Heapsort is not a stable sort — it does not preserve the relative order of equal elements.

heapsort-siftdown-bounded-by-height.text: Each siftDown call in heapsort is bounded by the tree height: floor(log₂ n) iterations. siftDown is the core primitive — it repairs a heap where only the root may violate the heap property.

heapsort-two-phases.text: Heapsort works in two phases: (1) build a max-heap from the input array in O(n) using Floyd's bottom-up construction, (2) repeatedly extract the maximum element (swap root with last unsorted element, sift-down) in O(n log n) total.

heapsort-vs-quicksort-practice.text: Heapsort is typically 2-3x slower than quicksort in practice due to poor cache locality and branch prediction behavior, despite heapsort's guaranteed O(n log n) worst case vs quicksort's O(n²) worst case.

implicit-array-tree-dual-efficiency.text: Array-implicit tree storage (binary heaps, Fenwick trees) achieves dual efficiency gains from a single design choice: encoding tree structure via arithmetic indexing eliminates pointer overhead (space efficiency) and ensures parent-child relationships map to sequential memory locations (cache efficiency) — both benefits are inherent consequences of replacing pointers with index formulas.

justifications.label: array-implicit foundation (d1) captures space efficiency; cache-friendly encoding (d1) captures locality — the dual benefit emerges from the same underlying encoding choice

incidence-matrix-poor-complexity.text: The incidence matrix representation uses O(|V| · |E|) space and has O(|V| · |E|) cost for every mutating operation, making it almost never the optimal choice

inorder-bst-sorted.text: In-order traversal (LNR) of a binary search tree visits keys in ascending sorted order; reverse in-order (RNL) visits keys in descending order.

interval-query-dual-extension-paths.text: The interval query landscape extends BST-based computation along two complementary paths: structural augmentation adds metadata to standard BSTs for overlap queries (each node stores max endpoint of its subtree), while specialized range structures (Fenwick trees for minimal-overhead prefix queries, segment trees for maximum-generality stabbing queries) build purpose-designed hierarchies — together covering the complete spectrum from point lookups through interval containment to aggregate range computation.

justifications.label: Augmentation and specialization are complementary paths from BSTs to interval query coverage

interval-query-structure-tradeoff.text: Interval query structures present a space-generality tradeoff: interval trees achieve O(n) space for 1-D stabbing queries, segment trees pay O(n log n) space but generalize cleanly to d dimensions via multi-level nesting, and Fenwick trees offer the simplest implementation for the special case of prefix-sum queries — each trades generality for either space or simplicity.

justifications.label: Three range-query structures occupy distinct points on the space-generality-simplicity trade surface

interval-tree-complexity.text: Interval tree complexity: O(n log n) build time, O(n) space, O(log n + m) query time, O(log n) insert/delete. The centered tree generalizes to higher dimensions with O(n log n) space.

interval-tree-output-sensitive.text: An interval tree answers overlap queries (find all intervals containing a query point) in O(log n + m) time where m is the number of results reported. This is output-sensitive and asymptotically optimal, vs O(n) for brute force.

interval-tree-two-designs.text: Two principal interval tree designs exist: the centered interval tree (recursively partitions around a center point, stores overlapping intervals in two sorted lists) and the augmented tree (BST keyed by low endpoint, each node annotated with max high endpoint in subtree — described in CLRS Section 14.3).

introsort-complete-inplace-comparison-so.text: Introsort is the complete in-place comparison sort: it achieves O(n log n) worst-case time (via heapsort fallback), O(log n) space (via tail-call optimization), and quicksort-level practical speed (via median-of-three pivoting) — resolving every dimension of the comparison-sort trilemma except stability.

justifications.label: Introsort inherits quicksort's instability, leaving merge sort as the necessary complement for order-preserving applications

introsort-hybrid.text: Introsort begins with quicksort and switches to heapsort when recursion depth exceeds a threshold, guaranteeing O(n log n) worst-case time while retaining quicksort's practical speed.

introsort-hybrid-guarantee.text: Introsort achieves O(n log n) worst-case with quicksort-level practical performance by using quicksort as the fast path and switching to heapsort when recursion depth exceeds O(log n), preventing quicksort's quadratic degeneration.

justifications.label: quicksort and heapsort perspectives on the same hybrid algorithm confirm the guarantee mechanism

introsort-resolves-comparison-trilemma.text: Introsort resolves the comparison-sort trilemma for the in-place+fast case: it achieves O(n log n) worst-case with quicksort's practical speed by hybridizing the two non-stable candidates, leaving only stability as the unavoidable sacrifice.

justifications.label: introsort eliminates the worst-case tradeoff axis from the three-way comparison-sort tension

kadane-algorithm-linear.text: Kadane's algorithm solves the maximum subarray problem in O(n) time and O(1) space using a single-pass scan with two variables: current_sum (best sum ending at current position) and best_sum (global best). This is optimal since any algorithm must read the entire input.

kadane-empty-vs-nonempty.text: Kadane's algorithm has two variants: (1) no empty subarrays allowed — initialize best_sum = -inf, use max(x, current_sum + x); (2) empty subarrays allowed — initialize best_sum = 0, use max(0, current_sum + x). The difference is a common source of exam questions.

kadane-exemplifies-paradigm-progression.text: Kadane's algorithm exemplifies how algorithmic paradigm shifts yield exponential improvements on a single problem: the maximum subarray problem progressed from O(n^3) brute force through O(n log n) divide-and-conquer to O(n) dynamic programming, with each step enabled by recognizing additional exploitable structure.

justifications.label: The progression from brute force to D&C to DP on one concrete problem mirrors the general paradigm hierarchy

kadane-instantiates-paradigm-spectrum.text: Kadane's algorithm illustrates the paradigm spectrum described by the backtracking-DP-greedy hierarchy: the maximum subarray problem progressed from O(n³) brute force through O(n log n) divide-and-conquer to O(n) dynamic programming, with each step enabled by recognizing additional exploitable structure. This progression is consistent with the trajectory from exhaustive search toward increasingly efficient paradigms that exploit problem-specific properties, though the antecedents do not establish that every transition maps one-to-one onto the theoretical hierarchy or that the intermediate O(n²) prefix-sum step fits neatly into the paradigm spectrum.

justifications.label: Maximum subarray concretely instantiates each level of the abstract paradigm spectrum on a single problem

kadane-recurrence.text: Kadane's key recurrence: current_sum[j] = max(A[j], current_sum[j-1] + A[j]) — at each position, decide whether to extend the previous subarray or start a new one. Then best_sum = max(best_sum, current_sum[j]).

kahns-vs-dfs-topo-sort.text: Kahn's algorithm detects cycles by checking if edges remain after processing all zero-indegree nodes; DFS-based topological sort detects cycles via temporary marks (back edges) and prepends nodes to the output list.

karatsuba-disproved-kolmogorov.text: Karatsuba's algorithm (1960) disproved Kolmogorov's conjecture that integer multiplication requires Ω(n²) operations, achieving O(n^1.585) via divide and conquer with 3 sub-multiplications of half-size operands

karatsuba-sub-quadratic.text: Karatsuba multiplication is the simplest sub-quadratic multiplication algorithm, reducing integer multiplication from O(n²) to O(n^log₂3) ≈ O(n^1.585) by trading one multiplication for additions.

knapsack-01-recurrence.text: The 0-1 knapsack recurrence: m[i,w] = max(m[i-1,w], m[i-1,w-w_i] + v_i) when w_i <= w; m[i,w] = m[i-1,w] when w_i > w. Base case: m[0,w] = 0. Each item is either taken or skipped.

knapsack-complexity-landscape.text: The knapsack problem occupies a unique position in computational complexity: it is NP-complete (weakly), admits a pseudo-polynomial DP solution in O(nW), AND has a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme — making it one of the rare NP-complete problems that is both practically solvable and theoretically approximable.

justifications.label: knapsack's triple nature — NP-complete yet pseudo-polynomial yet FPTAS — is uniquely tractable

knapsack-dp-pseudo-polynomial.text: The 0-1 knapsack DP solution runs in O(nW) time and O(nW) space. This is pseudo-polynomial, not polynomial, because W is exponential in its bit-length (log W bits). Space is reducible to O(W) if only the optimal value (not item selection) is needed.

knapsack-fptas-exists.text: The knapsack problem admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS), which uses the pseudo-polynomial DP as a subroutine. This distinguishes it from strongly NP-hard problems which have no FPTAS unless P=NP.

knapsack-illustrates-greedy-dp-boundary.text: The knapsack family is the canonical illustration of the greedy-to-DP optimization boundary: fractional knapsack admits a greedy O(n log n) solution because continuous relaxation preserves the greedy property, while 0-1 knapsack's integrality constraint breaks local-implies-global optimality and forces full DP at pseudo-polynomial cost. The same problem structure, differing only in integrality, crosses the NP-hardness boundary.

justifications.label: Fractional vs 0-1 knapsack is the sharpest known example of the greedy/DP boundary — same objective, same constraints, but integrality changes the complexity class

knapsack-three-variants.text: Three main knapsack variants: 0-1 (each item included or not, x_i in {0,1}), bounded (up to c copies, x_i in {0,...,c}), unbounded (unlimited copies, x_i in natural numbers). The unbounded variant has a simpler 1D DP: m[w] = max(v_i + m[w-w_i]).

knapsack-weakly-np-complete.text: The knapsack problem (decision version) is NP-complete. With integer weights/profits it is weakly NP-complete (admits pseudo-polynomial time solution). With rational weights/profits it is strongly NP-complete but still admits an FPTAS.

kruskal-complexity.text: Kruskal's algorithm has time complexity O(E log V) with comparison sort, equivalent to O(E log E) since log E = Θ(log V) for graphs without isolated vertices. Space complexity is O(V + E).

kruskal-definition.text: Kruskal's algorithm is a greedy algorithm that finds a minimum spanning tree (or forest for disconnected graphs) by repeatedly adding the lowest-weight edge that does not create a cycle, using a disjoint-set (union-find) data structure for cycle detection.

kruskal-mst-edge-count.text: Kruskal's algorithm produces exactly V-1 edges for a connected graph with V vertices. For disconnected graphs it produces a minimum spanning forest with one tree per connected component.

kruskal-presorted-complexity.text: When edges are pre-sorted or have small integer weights (enabling counting/radix sort), Kruskal's complexity drops to O(E · α(V)), dominated by union-find operations rather than sorting.

kruskal-sparse-vs-prim-dense.text: Kruskal's algorithm is optimal for sparse graphs; Prim's algorithm (with Fibonacci heap) is better for dense graphs.

laplacian-matrix-definition.text: The Laplacian matrix of a graph is L = D - A, where D is the diagonal degree matrix and A is the adjacency matrix; its eigenvalues are studied in spectral graph theory

lcs-diff-backbone.text: LCS is the algorithmic backbone of diff utilities, patch, and merge operations in version control systems like Git. The LCS DP table directly produces a diff by tracing diagonal moves (match), up moves (deletion), and left moves (insertion).

lcs-dp-complexity.text: The longest common subsequence (LCS) of two sequences of lengths m and n can be computed in O(mn) time and O(mn) space using dynamic programming. Space can be reduced to O(min(m,n)) for length-only computation, but full table is needed for traceback.

lcs-dp-powers-version-control.text: The DP-computed LCS/edit-distance family is the algorithmic foundation of modern version control: diff computes LCS to identify unchanged regions, patch encodes the edit distance operations, and three-way merge reconciles parallel changes — all reducible to the same O(mn) dynamic programming recurrence, making DP's ability to unify LCS, SCS, and edit distance practically consequential for every developer's daily workflow.

justifications.label: LCS/edit-distance unification (d1) shows theoretical interreducibility; diff-backbone shows the practical application — together they demonstrate DP powering a critical software infrastructure

lcs-edit-distance-unification.text: LCS, shortest common supersequence, and edit distance are three views of the same string similarity structure: |SCS| = m + n - |LCS|, and edit distance with only insertions and deletions equals m + n - 2|LCS| — solving any one solves the others.

justifications.label: LCS, SCS, and edit distance are interreducible via simple arithmetic relationships

lcs-general-np-hard.text: The LCS problem for an arbitrary number of sequences is NP-hard. For a fixed number N of sequences, dynamic programming gives O(N · product of all sequence lengths).

lcs-not-unique.text: The longest common subsequence is not necessarily unique — multiple LCSs of the same maximum length may exist. The number of common subsequences can be exponential, making enumeration of all LCSs non-polynomial.

lcs-optimal-substructure.text: LCS exhibits optimal substructure: if both sequences end with the same character, extend LCS of shorter prefixes; if they end with different characters, take the longer of the two subproblems dropping one character from each sequence.

lcs-scs-edit-distance.text: LCS relates to other problems: shortest common supersequence |SCS(X,Y)| = n + m - |LCS(X,Y)|; edit distance with only insertions and deletions (no substitution) d'(X,Y) = n + m - 2·|LCS(X,Y)|.

linear-sort-pipeline-requires-stability.text: The linear-time non-comparison sorting pipeline (radix sort via counting sort subroutine) achieves Θ(d(n+k)) time ONLY because counting sort preserves prior-digit ordering through its stability property; switching to the in-place counting sort variant destroys this stability guarantee and breaks the entire multi-pass pipeline's correctness.

justifications.label: Radix sort's linear-time guarantee depends on counting sort stability; in-place counting sort variant breaks the pipeline

linked-list-access-o-n.text: Linked list access is O(n) — sequential traversal only, no random access. Arrays have superior cache locality because linked list nodes are scattered in memory.

linked-list-complete-design-taxonomy.text: The linked list supports a rich design space organized along two complementary dimensions: structural variety (three orthogonal axes of link direction, circularity, and sentinel usage that compose independently to generate a family of list variants) and space optimization (pointer-reuse techniques including Morris traversal's temporary threading and XOR-linking's address arithmetic), illustrating that even a simple sequential structure admits systematic structural and space-efficiency trade-offs.

justifications.label: Structural axes (depth 1) and optimization techniques (depth 1) are orthogonal dimensions that together reveal the full scope of linked list design

linked-list-insert-delete-o1.text: Linked list insertion/deletion at a known position is O(1) requiring only pointer reassignment. However, finding that position requires O(n) traversal. In singly linked lists, deletion requires a pointer to the previous node; doubly linked lists can delete given only the node's address.

linked-list-orthogonal-design-axes.text: Linked list design involves three orthogonal structural choices that compose independently: link direction (singly vs doubly — trading one pointer per node for bidirectional traversal), topology (linear vs circular — trading a null terminator for O(1) tail-to-head wraparound), and boundary handling (sentinel nodes — trading one dummy node for eliminating null-check edge cases in insertion and deletion).

justifications.label: Three independent design axes compose to span the linked list design space

linked-list-tail-sharing.text: Tail-sharing (multiple lists sharing a common suffix) is exclusive to singly linked linear lists — a form of persistent data structure. Doubly linked and circular lists cannot share structure this way.

lookup-three-paradigm-landscape.text: The lookup landscape partitions into three complementary paradigms by key structure: hash tables provide O(1) unordered access (optimal when ordering is unnecessary), balanced BSTs provide O(log n) ordered access (required for range queries and sorted iteration), and tries provide O(m) string-specialized access (eliminating both the O(log n) comparison factor of BSTs and the collision risk of hashing) — a complete coverage where each paradigm dominates for its key-type and query-pattern regime.

justifications.label: The hash/BST duality partitions by ordering requirement; tries add a third regime where key structure (strings with shared prefixes) enables an approach superior to both — extending the two-way partition to a three-way coverage.

master-theorem-explains-dnc-complexity.text: The Master Theorem provides a closed-form bridge from divide-and-conquer recursion structure to time complexity: merge sort's T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n resolves to O(n log n), Karatsuba's 3T(n/2) + O(n) resolves to O(n^1.585), demonstrating how the sub-problem count directly determines whether D&C improves on naive algorithms.

justifications.label: Two concrete D&C recurrences illustrate the Master Theorem as the universal complexity calculator for the paradigm

mastery-competences-concretely-exercisab.text: Two of the three mastery competences are concretely exercisable through specific canon artifacts spanning complementary dimensions: correctness verification partitions cleanly by paradigm (exchange argument for greedy, induction for DP, precondition analysis for search), while hardware codesign pervades from representation level (graph adjacency structure) through data structures (balance strictness) to algorithms (cache-oblivious DnC) — making both competences not abstract requirements but demonstrably instantiated across the canon's full vertical extent.

justifications.label: Combines the verification and hardware threads to show that mastery competences have concrete instantiations, not just theoretical definitions.

mastery-competences-map-to-architecture.text: The three independent mastery competences (paradigm awareness, correctness verification, hardware codesign) appear to align with the three layers of the computational architecture: paradigm awareness relates to the paradigm layer (greedy, DP, exhaustive), hardware codesign relates to the substrate layer (arrays, trees), and correctness verification potentially spans layers through paradigm-specific proof techniques — suggesting the computational architecture may serve not only as a descriptive model of algorithmic structure but also as a possible framework for organizing learning.

justifications.label: Three mastery dimensions align with three architectural layers

mastery-paradigm-aware-dual-competence.text: Algorithm mastery requires paradigm-aware dual competence: the paradigm spectrum (brute-force → DP → greedy) concretely instantiated by Kadane and knapsack progressions defines WHAT structural insight is needed at each level, while the orthogonal correctness/performance rigor framework defines HOW to verify that insight is correctly applied — together they establish that mastery means knowing both which paradigm to apply and how to prove it works.

justifications.label: Mastery's two dimensions (correctness + structural insight) gain concrete meaning when mapped onto the paradigm spectrum: each paradigm level demands a specific kind of structural insight AND a corresponding verification technique.

mastery-requires-correctness-and-structu.text: Algorithm mastery demands simultaneous command of two independent dimensions: correctness verification (multi-level, from preconditions through implementation details like integer overflow) and structural insight (domain-specific knowledge that enables paradigm shifts from brute-force to optimal) — neither alone suffices, as a correct brute-force solution is practically inadequate while an incorrect optimal one is logically unsound.

justifications.label: Orthogonal rigor and structural insight are jointly necessary for algorithmic competence

mastery-three-independent-competences.text: Full algorithm mastery requires three independent competences that cannot substitute for each other: paradigm awareness (recognizing which point on the brute-force → greedy spectrum fits a problem), correctness methodology (applying the paradigm-specific proof technique), AND hardware-aware implementation (choosing data structure parameters that match the deployment memory tier) — extending the dual-competence model with a third dimension.

justifications.label: Theory, proof, and implementation are three independently necessary mastery dimensions

max-subarray-2d-cubic.text: The maximum sum rectangle in a 2D array is solvable in O(n³) time using Kadane's algorithm as a subroutine. A sub-cubic algorithm would imply a fast all-pairs shortest paths algorithm, suggesting this bound may be optimal.

max-subarray-historical-progression.text: Maximum subarray solutions progressed: O(n³) brute force → O(n²) prefix sums (Grenander) → O(n log n) divide and conquer (Shamos) → O(n) dynamic programming (Kadane). The problem was proposed by Grenander in 1977 as a simplified model for maximum likelihood estimation in digitized images.

memoization-automatic-via-hof.text: Automatic memoization can be applied externally to any referentially transparent function using higher-order functions, closures, or decorators, without modifying the original function.

memoization-bridges-recursion-and-dp.text: Memoization is the conceptual and computational bridge between recursion and dynamic programming: it transforms exponential multiple-recursion into polynomial time by caching overlapping subproblems, and this top-down cached recursion is formally dual to bottom-up tabulation — making any recursive formulation with overlapping subproblems automatically convertible to a DP solution via memoization as the intermediate step.

justifications.label: Memoization converts recursion into DP; the top-down/bottom-up duality means recursion + cache = tabulation

memoization-from-exponential-to-polynomi.text: Memoization achieves a qualitative complexity class shift — from exponential to polynomial — in two distinct domains: dynamic programming (reducing naive recursive Fibonacci from O(2^n) to O(n)) and parsing (reducing backtracking parsers from exponential to O(n^3)/O(n^4)), demonstrating that subproblem caching is a general-purpose complexity tamer.

justifications.label: Two independent exponential-to-polynomial reductions via memoization reveal a domain-general pattern

memoization-parsing-complexity.text: Memoization reduces exponential backtracking parsers to polynomial time: O(n³) for non-left-recursive grammars, O(n⁴) for left-recursive grammars (Frost, Hafiz, Callaghan 2007).

memoization-requires-purity.text: Memoization requires referential transparency: only pure functions (no side effects) can be correctly memoized, because calling the function must have the same effect as substituting its return value.

memoization-runtime-not-compile-time.text: Memoization is a runtime optimization technique, distinct from compile-time optimizations such as strength reduction; it is machine-independent and cross-platform.

memoization-tames-multiple-recursion.text: Memoization transforms multiple recursion from exponential to polynomial by caching overlapping subproblems, making it the essential bridge between recursive problem formulation and tractable computation.

justifications.label: Multiple recursion's exponential blowup arises from recomputation of overlapping subproblems; memoization eliminates precisely this redundancy

memoization-top-down-dp.text: Memoization is the top-down counterpart to bottom-up dynamic programming; both cache subproblem results to avoid redundant computation.

memoization-universal-optimization-bridg.text: Memoization universally transforms exponential recursive computations into polynomial dynamic programming solutions, serving as the bridge from naive recursion to efficient DP across both algorithmic domains (Fibonacci, knapsack) and parsing (backtracking parsers to polynomial packrat parsers).

justifications.label: Memoization's universality breaks down for impure functions — side effects make cached results incorrect, gating the exponential-to-polynomial transformation

mergesort-all-case-nlogn.text: Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) time complexity in all cases: worst, average, and best.

mergesort-complexity.text: Merge sort runs in O(n log n) in all cases (best, average, worst), requires O(n) extra memory, is stable, and is highly parallelizable.

mergesort-external-sorting.text: Merge sort is the standard algorithm for external sorting (data too large for memory), used with tape drives or disk via k-way merge; a basic 4-tape version requires log₂(n) passes.

mergesort-recurrence.text: Merge sort's recurrence relation is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, solved by the master theorem to O(n log n).

mergesort-space-complexity.text: Merge sort requires O(n) auxiliary space for array implementations; linked-list implementations need only O(1) auxiliary space plus O(log n) stack space.

mergesort-stable.text: Merge sort is stable: equal elements retain their original relative order in most implementations. This is a key differentiator from quicksort and heapsort.

mergesort-unqualified-stable-sort.text: Merge sort is the unqualified default when a stable O(n log n) comparison sort is needed — uniquely stable among its peers, with guaranteed worst-case performance and optimal comparison count.

justifications.label: Merge sort's unique stability and guaranteed O(n log n) make it the default stable sort, qualified only by its O(n) auxiliary space requirement which disqualifies it for space-constrained environments

mergesort-vs-quicksort.text: Merge sort's worst case uses ~39% fewer comparisons than quicksort's average case. Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) while quicksort degrades to O(n²) worst case, but quicksort has better cache locality on arrays.

modular-arithmetic-bounded-resource-prim.text: Modular arithmetic is the canonical implementation technique for bounded cyclic resources across memory and protocol domains: circular buffers use index mod n for O(1) bounded queue operations with wraparound, and sliding window protocols use sequence number mod N for bounded transmission tracking — the same cyclic group structure enables constant-time wraparound management wherever a finite resource space must be reused indefinitely

justifications.label: Modular arithmetic solves bounded-resource wraparound in both data structures and network protocols

modular-arithmetic-universal-bounded-acc.text: Modular arithmetic is the universal mechanism for bounded sequential access across abstraction levels: circular buffers use index mod n for O(1) bounded-capacity queues in memory, and sliding window protocols use sequence number mod N for reliable ordered delivery over unreliable links — the same cyclic group structure solves bounded sequential access at both the data structure and network protocol layers.

justifications.label: Same modular arithmetic structure underlies bounded access in both memory queues and network protocols

morris-traversal-o1-space.text: Morris traversal performs in-order tree traversal in O(1) extra space by temporarily repurposing null child pointers as threading links to the in-order predecessor/successor, then restoring the tree structure. It cannot support concurrent traversals.

morris-traversal-proves-stack-eliminabil.text: Morris traversal demonstrates that tree traversal's apparent dependence on an auxiliary stack can be circumvented in specific cases: by temporarily threading null child pointers as traversal links, it achieves complete in-order traversal in O(1) extra space. This suggests that tree structure itself can encode sufficient navigational information to replace the O(h) auxiliary stack in at least some traversal scenarios, though the technique's limitations (e.g., no concurrent traversals, in-order only) mean it does not generalize to eliminating stack dependence across all patterns where LIFO discipline is foundational — such as arbitrary DFS, backtracking search, or expression evaluation.

justifications.label: Morris traversal eliminates the stack dependency for tree traversal by repurposing tree structure itself

mst-algorithm-portfolio.text: The MST problem has a complementary algorithm portfolio: Kruskal's (edge-sort-dominated at O(E log V), optimal for sparse graphs) and Prim's (priority-queue-driven, optimal for dense graphs with Fibonacci heap at O(E + V log V)) — with union-find making Kruskal's sort-bottlenecked and Fibonacci heap making Prim's decrease-key-free.

justifications.label: Kruskal and Prim partition MST optimality by graph density with different enabling data structures

mst-shortest-path-shared-infrastructure-.text: MST and single-source shortest path share implementation infrastructure (Fibonacci-heap PQ, greedy extraction loop, O(|E|+|V| log |V|) via Prim/Dijkstra) yet diverge in theoretical structure: shortest path is unified under the Bellman equation as a DP problem with greedy specializations, while MST has a complementary algorithm portfolio (Kruskal for sparse, Prim for dense) justified by the cut property rather than dynamic programming optimality.

justifications.label: MST and shortest path share PQ infrastructure but differ in theoretical foundation (cut property vs Bellman equation)

mst-sp-infrastructure-convergence-via-pr.text: The Prim-Dijkstra shared infrastructure (triple parallelism concretized in shared Fibonacci heap) is the implementation-level explanation for why MST and shortest path share infrastructure despite divergent theory: the two problems converge on the same greedy extraction loop and priority queue because both reduce to minimum-weight frontier selection, even though their correctness derives from different principles (cut property vs. Bellman equation).

justifications.label: Shared Fibonacci heap infrastructure (depth-4) explains the infrastructure-theory divergence (depth-6) — same implementation, different mathematics

natural-mergesort-best-case.text: Natural merge sort exploits pre-existing sorted runs in the input, achieving O(n) best-case time on already-sorted data with a single pass.

negative-weight-complete-and-dp-unified.text: The negative-weight shortest path landscape achieves both completeness and theoretical unity: completeness at both cardinality levels (Bellman-Ford for single-source, Floyd-Warshall for all-pairs) and unity under the Bellman equation (both are DP decompositions along different dimensions — by path length and by intermediate vertices) — making negative weights the specific domain where DP's unifying power is most clearly demonstrated.

justifications.label: Cardinality completeness (depth-4) plus DP unification (depth-3) shows negative-weight shortest paths as DP's strongest unity demonstration

negative-weight-landscape-complete-both-.text: The negative-weight shortest path landscape is theory-practice complete at both cardinality levels: single-source is fully addressed by Bellman-Ford (with negative cycle detection, SPFA queue optimization, and early termination), and all-pairs is fully addressed by Floyd-Warshall (with path reconstruction via predecessor matrix and transitive closure as a Boolean specialization), achieving completeness through complementary practical augmentations at each scale.

justifications.label: Single-source (Bellman-Ford) and all-pairs (Floyd-Warshall) each achieve theory-practice completeness independently

negative-weight-landscape-crowns-dp-unif.text: The negative-weight shortest path landscape — complete at both cardinality levels and unified under the Bellman equation — represents the strongest evidence for DP's centrality claim: it is precisely in the domain where greedy algorithms fail (negative weights) that DP's unifying power is most clearly demonstrated, and this landscape's completeness validates DP's role as the boundary-extending technique that expands the canon's problem coverage beyond what greedy alone can reach.

justifications.label: Negative-weight completeness (depth-5) validates DP's boundary-extension role in structural irreplaceability (depth-11) — the hardest shortest-path domain is where DP's unique value is proven

negative-weight-shortest-path-portfolio.text: Two classical algorithms handle negative edge weights: Bellman-Ford for single-source (O(|V||E|)) and Floyd-Warshall for all-pairs (O(|V|³)); Dijkstra cannot serve either role when negative weights are present.

justifications.label: depth-2 — Dijkstra's exclusion from negative weights forces selection between the two alternatives
repair: linked Bellman-Ford is a single-source shortest-path algo

negative-weight-shortest-path-stratified.text: Negative-weight shortest paths admit meaningful speedups when structural properties are available: DAGs allow O(|V|+|E|) via topological-order DP (faster than both Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford), while general graphs require O(|V|·|E|) Bellman-Ford for single-source or O(|V|³) Floyd-Warshall for all-pairs — suggesting that exploiting acyclicity can yield order-of-magnitude improvements even within the negative-weight regime.

justifications.label: DAG structure enables linear-time negative-weight shortest paths; general graphs require polynomial algorithms

non-comparison-sort-enables-linear-krusk.text: When edge weights are small integers, non-comparison sorts (counting/radix) sort edges in O(|E|) time, reducing Kruskal's algorithm to O(|E| · α(|V|)) — dominated entirely by union-find rather than sorting — demonstrating a concrete instance where the non-comparison sorting regime directly accelerates graph optimization beyond comparison-sort-bounded predictions.

justifications.label: Linear-time integer sorting shifts Kruskal's bottleneck from edge sorting to union-find

non-comparison-sort-family-uniformly-lin.text: The non-comparison sort family (counting sort, radix sort, bucket sort) uniformly achieves linear-time performance for bounded-range keys, making sub-O(n log n) sorting universally available whenever key values can serve as indices.

justifications.label: Bucket sort's O(n²) degeneration when elements cluster breaks the family's uniform linearity claim

non-comparison-sort-fast-lane-to-graph-o.text: The sorting-to-graph-optimization connection has a second, faster pathway beyond the main PQ pipeline: when edge weights have bounded integer range, non-comparison sorts (counting/radix) reduce Kruskal's sorting phase from O(|E| log |E|) to O(|E|), making the total MST cost O(|E| · α(|V|)) — dominated by union-find rather than sorting, and bypassing the priority queue mechanism entirely.

justifications.label: A fast lane through non-comparison sorting + Kruskal bypasses the PQ pipeline for bounded-weight MST

non-comparison-sort-linear.text: Non-comparison sorts (counting sort, radix sort, bucket sort) can achieve O(n) time, beating the Ω(n log n) lower bound for comparison-based sorting, but require assumptions about the input (e.g., bounded integer keys).

non-comparison-sorts-circumvent-lower-bo.text: Counting sort and radix sort both achieve sub-O(n log n) time by using key values as array indices rather than comparing elements, circumventing the Ω(n log n) comparison-sort lower bound that applies to merge sort, heapsort, and quicksort.

justifications.label: both algorithms exploit the same loophole in the comparison-sort lower bound

open-addressing-load-limit.text: Open addressing requires load factor α < 1 (table full at α = 1); practical optimal range is 0.6–0.75. Performance degrades sharply as α approaches 1

open-addressing-probe-sequences.text: Open addressing uses three probe sequence strategies: linear probing (fixed interval, susceptible to primary clustering), quadratic probing (quadratic polynomial intervals), and double hashing (interval from secondary hash function)

operational-coverage-grounds-mastery-fra.text: The canon's broad operational coverage (traversal activating all three architecture layers combined with data access via three complementary paradigms) provides a strong computational substrate supporting the mastery framework: the three mastery competences (paradigm awareness, correctness verification, hardware codesign) map onto the three-layer architecture and operate on the 2×2 content organization, and broad operational coverage reduces the likelihood that mastery gaps arise from missing operational capability — the operations are available to practice the identified skills.

justifications.label: Operational completeness (depth 8) and mastery-content alignment (depth 9) share three-layer architecture as common foundation, revealing operations as the substrate enabling mastery

optimization-paradigm-single-monotonic-p.text: The algorithmic optimization landscape exhibits a broadly monotonic progression from greater generality toward greater efficiency: naive recursion → memoization → dynamic programming → greedy, where each transition tends to trade problem coverage for computational efficiency. This progression is theoretically motivated (each stage can be viewed as a restriction of its predecessor) and is illustrated by problems like maximum subarray, though the progression is not strictly linear across all problem domains—greedy algorithms require specific structural properties (local optimality guaranteeing global optimality) rather than being a universal next step from DP.

justifications.label: The recursion-to-greedy pipeline (d3) and backtracking-to-greedy spectrum (d3) are two views of the same monotonic progression — unifying them reveals a single axis from generality to efficiency.

optimization-via-progressive-refinement-.text: The algorithms canon exhibits two independent progressive refinement patterns that together span the full optimization landscape: the amortized-to-worst-case refinement converts probabilistic or averaged guarantees into deterministic ones (Fibonacci to Brodal heaps, two-stack to real-time queues), while recursion elimination converts space-intensive recursive patterns into efficient iterative ones (single recursion to iteration, multiple recursion to memoization to DP) — each progressing from easy-to-achieve-but-weaker to hard-to-achieve-but-stronger guarantees along orthogonal axes.

justifications.label: Two independent refinement patterns (time guarantee strengthening and space/control-flow optimization) share the same progressive structure but operate on orthogonal dimensions.

ordered-access-mechanism-independent.text: Logarithmic ordered access is a fundamental consequence of hierarchical ordering itself rather than any specific balancing mechanism: binary search operationalizes the ordering invariant into computational power through any sorted hierarchy, and skip lists independently validate that this same power emerges from randomized hierarchy construction — demonstrating that O(log n) ordered access is an intrinsic property of layered structure, not an artifact of deterministic tree balancing

justifications.label: Both deterministic and randomized hierarchies yield logarithmic access, proving mechanism independence

ordered-data-structure-spectrum.text: Ordered data access forms a four-tier implementation spectrum with increasing key-type generality: arrays with binary search (O(log n), integers/comparable), balanced BSTs (O(log n), in-order traversal + dynamic), tries (O(m), string-native sorted order), and hash tables (O(1) average but NO ordered operations) — the choice is governed by whether ordered queries are needed.

justifications.label: The lookup-structure landscape divides cleanly on whether ordered operations are required

ordering-and-traversal-dual-universal-me.text: The algorithms canon has two universal operational mechanisms forming a what/how duality: ordering defines what is preserved (BST ordering for search, heap ordering for priority, sorted ordering for binary search), while traversal defines how structure is activated (processing elements across all architecture layers, enabling the paradigm hierarchy) — one governs invariants, the other governs execution.

justifications.label: The universal invariant (ordering, depth-7) and the universal primitive (traversal, depth-4) are complementary — invariant vs activation

ordering-unifies-tree-computation.text: Ordering serves as a primary unifying principle of tree computation: BST operations (search, insert, delete) share a common reduction to the in-order relationship, and traversal semantics (sorted output, prefix/postfix notation, tree reconstruction) are determined by traversal order choice — with two traversal sequences being informationally equivalent to the original tree. The BST ordering invariant and traversal order are thus deeply connected aspects of the same underlying structure.

justifications.label: BST operations reduce to ordering; traversal semantics are determined by ordering — ordering is the single unifying principle

ordering-universal-invariant-across-scal.text: Ordering serves as the canon's universal computational invariant operating at three complementary scales: within individual trees, the BST ordering invariant unifies search, deletion, and successor operations into a single structural principle; across collections, sorting creates the precondition enabling binary search's O(log n) lookup on arbitrary datasets; and across paradigms, the three lookup paradigms (hash for unordered O(1), BST for ordered O(log n), trie for sequential O(m)) partition precisely by how they exploit or discard ordering structure.

justifications.label: Tree-internal ordering + collection-level ordering + paradigm-differentiating ordering = universal invariant across scales

packrat-parsing-linear-time.text: Packrat parsing (Ford 2002) uses memoization to guarantee linear-time parsing of Parsing Expression Grammars (PEGs).

paradigm-spectrum-predictive-and-prescri.text: The paradigm spectrum (brute-force → DP → greedy) is the canon's central organizing principle along two independent axes: it is predictive of algorithmic structure (correctly forecasting string algorithm bifurcation by tractability class) and prescriptive of verification methodology (each paradigm position determines the appropriate correctness proof technique via paradigm-specific dual-axis rigor), unifying algorithm discovery and algorithm validation under a single framework.

justifications.label: The paradigm spectrum's predictive power (depth 6, string bifurcation) and prescriptive power (depth 8, verification methodology) are independently derived, revealing it as a unified discovery-and-validation framework

paradigm-spectrum-predictive-framework.text: The brute-force → greedy paradigm spectrum is concretely instantiated by two problem families: Kadane's maximum subarray progression demonstrates exponential speedups from paradigm shifts on a single problem (O(n³) to O(n)), while the knapsack family illustrates how a problem's position on the spectrum correlates with its tractability via pruning, DP structure, and matroid properties — making it a diagnostic and illustrative framework supported by these specific examples, though its generality as a complete predictive tool remains to be established beyond these cases.

justifications.label: Depth-5 synthesis elevating the paradigm spectrum from descriptive taxonomy to predictive tool

perfect-hash-function-definition.text: A perfect hash function is injective on the key set S (every key maps to a unique index with zero collisions); only possible when all keys are known in advance

pillars-doubly-connected-via-dp-and-pipe.text: The algorithms canon's two pillars (graph optimization and sorting/computation) are doubly connected: structurally via the sorting→PQ→Dijkstra/Prim implementation pipeline and conceptually via DP's universal theoretical reach across both domains — making them a tightly coupled system rather than merely adjacent fields.

justifications.label: Two independent depth-7 cross-pillar connections (implementation pipeline and DP universality) combine to show the pillars are doubly bound

planarity-three-characterizations.text: Three classical theorems characterize planar graphs from complementary perspectives: Wagner's theorem specifies WHEN a graph is planar (if and only if it has no K_5 or K_3,3 minor), Fary's theorem shows HOW planar graphs embed (straight-line edges always suffice), and the four-color theorem reveals what planarity ENABLES (at most 4 colors needed for proper coloring) — together providing a complete existence/construction/consequence characterization.

justifications.label: Three theorems give complementary when/how/what characterizations of planar graphs

pointer-reuse-space-elimination.text: A recurring design pattern in linked structures eliminates auxiliary space by repurposing pointer fields for dual duty: Morris traversal temporarily converts null child pointers into threading links to achieve O(1)-space tree traversal without a stack, while XOR-linking permanently encodes two pointers (prev and next) in a single field to implement doubly-linked traversal with singly-linked space — both sacrifice implementation simplicity and concurrent-access safety for space savings.

justifications.label: Two independently conceived techniques share the structural principle of pointer-field reuse; their combination identifies a general pattern where auxiliary space can be eliminated by encoding multiple navigation relationships in the same storage.

pq-implementation-determines-graph-perfo.text: Priority queue implementation choice is a primary factor in graph algorithm performance: the PQ spectrum from unsorted arrays through binary heaps to Fibonacci heaps offers different insert/extract/decrease-key tradeoffs, and Fibonacci heaps' O(1) amortized decrease-key makes greedy graph algorithms like Dijkstra and Prim edge-dominated rather than queue-dominated. Matching PQ implementation to graph density is among the key design decisions influencing whether these algorithms approach asymptotically optimal performance for a given graph class.

justifications.label: The abstract PQ spectrum concretely instantiates as graph algorithm performance tiers — implementation choice IS performance choice

pq-unifies-sorting-and-graph-optimizatio.text: Priority queues connect sorting and graph optimization as a shared algorithmic theme: PQ implementations parallel sorting strategies (e.g., binary heap ↔ heapsort), and PQ choice is a primary factor in graph algorithm performance (array PQ → O(|V|²) Dijkstra/Prim, Fibonacci heap → O(|E| + |V| log |V|)). However, the evidence establishes these as two independent observations — that sorting is comprehensively resolved across practical regimes and that PQ implementation governs graph performance tiers — without demonstrating a direct causal link between the resolution of sorting and the resolution of graph optimization.

justifications.label: Priority queue implementations bridge sorting theory to graph algorithm practice; solving one domain transitively solved the other

preorder-copy-postorder-delete.text: Pre-order traversal is used to copy a tree (parent created before children); post-order traversal is used to delete a tree (children freed before parent).

preorder-prefix-postorder-postfix.text: Pre-order traversal of an expression tree produces prefix notation (Polish notation); post-order traversal produces postfix notation (Reverse Polish notation), which is directly translatable to stack machine code.

prim-adjacency-matrix-complexity.text: Prim's algorithm with adjacency matrix and linear search runs in O(|V|²) total time.

prim-binary-heap-complexity.text: Prim's algorithm with binary heap and adjacency list runs in O(|E| log |V|) total time.

prim-cut-property-correctness.text: Prim's algorithm correctness relies on the cut property: the lightest edge crossing any cut of a graph must belong to some minimum spanning tree.

prim-definition.text: Prim's algorithm is a greedy algorithm that finds a minimum spanning tree by growing from an arbitrary starting vertex, always adding the cheapest edge crossing the cut between tree and non-tree vertices.

prim-dijkstra-correctness-parallel.text: Prim's and Dijkstra's structural near-identity extends from implementation to correctness proofs: both rely on a greedy invariant validated by extracting the priority queue minimum — the cut property proves the lightest crossing edge belongs to some MST (Prim), while the relaxation invariant proves visited nodes have final shortest distances (Dijkstra) — the same loop structure works because analogous proof structures apply.

justifications.label: Shared PQ-extraction loop correctness follows from analogous greedy invariants for MST and shortest path

prim-dijkstra-infrastructure-concretized.text: Prim and Dijkstra's triple parallelism (shared implementation loop, parallel correctness proofs, common DP-specialization theory) is supported by shared Fibonacci heap infrastructure: the same O(1) amortized decrease-key operation is a primary mechanism enabling both algorithms to achieve their optimal O(|E|+|V| log |V|) bound via priority-queue-driven greedy extraction, making the theoretical parallelism manifest in shared data-structure choices.

justifications.label: Triple parallelism (implementation, correctness, theory) converges on a single shared Fibonacci heap realization

prim-dijkstra-structural-similarity.text: Prim's algorithm is structurally almost identical to Dijkstra's: same priority-queue-based loop, but Prim relaxes edges by individual edge weight while Dijkstra relaxes by cumulative path cost.

prim-dijkstra-triple-parallelism.text: Prim and Dijkstra exhibit parallelism at three independent levels: implementation structure (same priority-queue-driven greedy extraction loop), correctness proof structure (both validated by greedy invariants — cut property for Prim, relaxation optimality for Dijkstra), and theoretical foundation (both are DP specializations where local optimality guarantees global optimality) — differing only in the relaxation criterion (edge weight vs cumulative path distance).

justifications.label: Implementation, proof, and theory all parallel — the algorithms differ only in what quantity is minimized

prim-dijkstra-unified-scope-bounded.text: The Prim-Dijkstra unified implementation pattern (shared Fibonacci-heap greedy extraction loop achieving O(|E|+|V| log |V|) for both MST and shortest path) covers the two primary weighted graph optimization problems in optimal time, but only within constrained scope.

justifications.label: The unified Prim-Dijkstra pattern achieves optimal weighted graph optimization unless negative weights break Dijkstra or disconnectedness breaks Prim

prim-fibonacci-heap-complexity.text: Prim's algorithm with Fibonacci heap and adjacency list runs in O(|E| + |V| log |V|) total time, achieving linear time on sufficiently dense graphs.

prim-optimal-dense-mst.text: Prim's algorithm with Fibonacci heap is the asymptotically fastest MST algorithm for dense graphs, achieving O(|E| + |V| log |V|) time.

justifications.label: Prim's density advantage applies only to connected graphs; disconnected graphs require Kruskal's

prim-requires-connected-graph.text: Prim's algorithm in its basic form works only on connected graphs, unlike Kruskal's and Borůvka's which find minimum spanning forests of disconnected graphs directly.

prim-vs-kruskal-density.text: Prim's algorithm is preferred over Kruskal's for dense graphs; Kruskal's is preferred for sparse graphs.

priority-queue-greedy-graph-backbone.text: Priority queues are the shared algorithmic backbone of Dijkstra's, Prim's, and A*: all three are greedy algorithms that repeatedly extract the minimum-cost frontier element, differing only in what cost function drives the queue.

justifications.label: three major graph algorithms unified by the same priority-queue-driven greedy loop

priority-queue-implementation-spectrum.text: A priority queue is an abstract data type with implementations spanning a performance spectrum — including unsorted arrays, sorted arrays, binary heaps, and Fibonacci heaps, each with different complexity tradeoffs — and the sorting equivalence theorem shows that each implementation induces a corresponding sorting algorithm (e.g., binary heap ↔ heapsort, unsorted array ↔ selection sort, sorted array ↔ insertion sort).

justifications.label: priority queue implementations and sorting algorithms are dually related

priority-queue-is-adt.text: A priority queue is an abstract data type (not a data structure); it can be implemented with unsorted arrays, sorted arrays, binary heaps, binomial heaps, Fibonacci heaps, or balanced BSTs, each with different complexity tradeoffs.

priority-queue-optimality-dual-guarantee.text: Priority queues admit two forms of optimal bounds: Fibonacci heaps achieve O(1) amortized insert and decrease-key (sufficient for Dijkstra/Prim optimality), while Brodal queues and strict Fibonacci heaps achieve the same O(1) bounds in the worst case (not amortized) — demonstrating that the priority queue abstraction supports both lazy/amortized and eager/worst-case implementation strategies at theoretically optimal performance.

justifications.label: Two independent results establish the same asymptotic bounds via different guarantee types; their combination reveals that priority queue optimality is achievable under both amortized and worst-case models.

priority-queue-sorting-equivalence.text: There is a deep equivalence between priority queues and sorting algorithms: using a priority queue to sort yields a comparison sort (heapsort ↔ binary heap, selection sort ↔ unsorted array, insertion sort ↔ sorted array, tree sort ↔ BST).

python-empty-set-literal.text: In Python, {} creates an empty dict, not an empty set; an empty set must be created with set().

queue-implementation-spectrum.text: Queue implementations span a three-tier spectrum trading capacity and mechanism complexity for guarantee strength: circular buffers provide O(1) worst-case for bounded queues via modular arithmetic, two-stack queues achieve O(1) amortized for unbounded queues via lazy transfer, and real-time queues achieve O(1) worst-case for unbounded queues via incremental lazy evaluation.

justifications.label: Three queue implementations demonstrate a bounded→amortized-unbounded→worst-case-unbounded progression

queue-instantiates-amortized-refinement-.text: The queue implementation spectrum is a concrete instance of the amortized-to-worst-case refinement pattern: circular buffers provide trivial bounded-capacity O(1), two-stack queues achieve amortized O(1) via lazy batch transfer, and real-time queues refine to worst-case O(1) via incremental schedule rotation, demonstrating the full refinement trajectory within a single ADT.

justifications.label: Queue implementations trace the exact amortized-to-worst-case refinement progression

quicksort-complexity.text: Quicksort has average-case time complexity O(n log n) and worst-case O(n²); the worst case occurs with poor pivot selection on sorted, reverse-sorted, or all-equal input (Lomuto scheme).

quicksort-history.text: Quicksort was invented by Tony Hoare in 1959 at Moscow State University and published in 1961 in Communications of the ACM.

quicksort-introsort.text: Introsort is a hybrid algorithm that starts with quicksort but switches to heapsort when recursion depth exceeds O(log n), guaranteeing O(n log n) worst-case time.

quicksort-lomuto-vs-hoare.text: Hoare's partition scheme performs approximately 3x fewer swaps on average than Lomuto's; Lomuto degrades to O(n²) on all-equal elements while Hoare produces balanced partitions.

quicksort-median-of-three.text: Median-of-three pivot selection reduces quicksort's expected comparisons from ~1.386n log n to ~1.188n log n, an approximately 14% reduction.

quicksort-not-stable.text: Quicksort is not a stable sort: the relative order of equal elements is not preserved in standard implementations.

quicksort-optimized-near-universal-sort.text: Quicksort with median-of-three pivot selection and three-way partitioning achieves near-universal practical superiority among comparison sorts: median-of-three reduces expected comparisons by approximately 14 percent, three-way partition handles duplicate-heavy inputs in O(n) best-case, and together they cover essentially all practical input distributions with the lowest constant factors — providing speed superiority across all distribution types that would make it the default sort everywhere.

justifications.label: Optimized quicksort dominates on pure speed, but instability disqualifies it from contexts requiring order preservation (radix sort subroutine, multi-key sorting, standard library defaults like Python's timsort).

quicksort-practical-default.text: Quicksort is the practical default comparison sort due to superior cache locality and constant factors, despite its O(n²) worst case — the worst case is the sole reason it isn't unconditionally dominant.

justifications.label: quicksort dominates in practice unless its quadratic worst case is triggered

quicksort-space-complexity.text: Quicksort uses O(log n) auxiliary space when recursing into the smaller partition first (Hoare's 1962 tail-call optimization); without this optimization it uses O(n) auxiliary space.

quicksort-three-way-partition.text: Three-way partition (Dutch National Flag) achieves O(n) best-case time when all elements are equal by partitioning into less-than, equal-to, and greater-than regions.

radix-counting-stable-sort-pipeline.text: Radix sort's linear-time guarantee depends on counting sort's stability: counting sort preserves prior-digit ordering as the per-digit subroutine, and this stability is what makes LSD radix sort correct — the pipeline is a stable-sort composition.

justifications.label: radix sort correctness is a direct consequence of counting sort stability

radix-sort-complexity.text: Radix sort has time complexity Θ(d(n+k)) where d is key length in digits, n is number of keys, and k is the range of each digit; space complexity is O(d+n).

radix-sort-counting-subroutine.text: LSD radix sort uses counting sort as a stable subroutine for each digit pass; Seward developed both algorithms together at MIT in 1954.

radix-sort-linear-time.text: When key length d is constant and digit range k = O(n), radix sort runs in linear time Θ(n).

radix-sort-lsd-stable.text: LSD (least significant digit) radix sort is inherently stable; in-place MSD variants including binary quicksort are not stable. Stable MSD requires O(n) auxiliary memory.

radix-sort-lsd-vs-msd.text: LSD processes digits from rightmost to leftmost producing natural integer ordering; MSD processes leftmost to rightmost producing lexicographic ordering and is naturally recursive with each bucket independently sub-sorted.

radix-sort-non-comparative.text: Radix sort is a non-comparative sorting algorithm that distributes elements into buckets by individual digit values, circumventing the Ω(n log n) comparison sort lower bound.

radix-tree-compressed-trie.text: A radix tree (compressed trie) merges single-child chain nodes into one node, saving space for sparse key sets. The Patricia tree is the binary-encoded variant using skip numbers to avoid empty subtrees.

range-query-complete-tradeoff-space.text: Range query data structures exhibit a simplicity-generality tradeoff: Fenwick trees achieve minimal overhead through elegant bit-manipulation encoding of three implicit trees in a single array, segment trees add support for arbitrary associative range operations at O(n log n) space cost, and interval trees achieve O(n) space for pure stabbing queries — together these three structures illustrate a spectrum from the simplest prefix-sum case to more general multi-dimensional range queries.

justifications.label: Fenwick (simple/fast) → segment tree (general) → interval tree (space-optimal) spans the complete range-query tradeoff

range-query-extends-tree-hardware-bridge.text: Range query data structures extend the tree-hardware bridge from point operations to aggregate queries: the same array-implicit and balanced-tree substrates that span the memory hierarchy for point access (heaps for priority, BSTs for sorted retrieval, B-trees for disk) also underpin the complete range query tradeoff space — Fenwick trees for prefix sums, segment trees for general interval aggregation, and interval trees for stabbing queries.

justifications.label: Range query structures inherit and extend the tree memory-hierarchy spanning established for point queries

realtime-queue-invariant.text: The real-time queue maintains the invariant |s| = |f| - |r|; when s is empty, |f| = |r| and a rotation is triggered.

realtime-queue-worst-case-o1.text: A real-time queue achieves worst-case O(1) for all operations using three lists (f, r, s) with lazy evaluation and memoization; the schedule list s incrementally forces computation so no single operation bears the full O(n) reversal cost.

recursion-elimination-complete-paradigm-.text: Recursion elimination constitutes a complete learnable pathway to algorithmic paradigm mastery: the elimination hierarchy (single recursion to iteration, multiple recursion to memoization/DP, structural recursion to termination guarantees) directly mirrors the paradigm efficiency progression (brute-force to DP to greedy), so systematically mastering recursion transformation IS acquiring paradigm awareness — UNLESS memoization's requirement for referential transparency limits the memoization-to-DP step to pure functions, making the pathway incomplete for effectful computations.

justifications.label: Recursion elimination equals paradigm mastery unless memoization purity requirement limits scope

recursion-elimination-mirrors-paradigm-p.text: The recursion elimination hierarchy corresponds directly to the paradigm efficiency progression: single recursion → iteration mirrors brute-force enumeration, multiple recursion → memoization mirrors the shift to DP, and the final DP → greedy step eliminates the subproblem table entirely — revealing that paradigm advancement IS systematically eliminating recursive structure.

justifications.label: Each paradigm shift corresponds to eliminating a tier of recursive structure

metadata.retract_reason: repair: abandoned — The mapping is fundamentally forced: it drops an entire tier (stack-based recursion) from one antecedent to make the correspondence work, and the claimed parallel between single recursion→iteration and brute-force enumeration is backwards. These aren't softening problems—the core thesis that paradigm advancement IS systematically eliminating recursive structure requires a clean structural correspondence that doesn't exist between these two antecedents. No amount of weakening fixes a mapping that must omit evidence to hold.

recursion-elimination-stratified-by-type.text: Recursion elimination is stratified into three tiers by recursion pattern: single recursion converts directly to iteration with O(1) auxiliary space, stack-based recursive patterns (DFS, backtracking) require an explicit stack as computational substrate with O(depth) space, and multiple recursion requires memoization or tabulation with polynomial cache space — each tier trades progressively more auxiliary space for handling fundamentally more complex recursive structures.

justifications.label: Three recursion types require progressively more space to eliminate: O(1), O(depth), O(subproblems)

recursion-first-languages.text: LISP (McCarthy, 1960) was the first language to use recursion as a core feature; ALGOL 60 independently added recursive procedure calls the same year.

recursion-to-greedy-optimization-pipelin.text: The full algorithmic optimization pipeline forms a monotonic efficiency progression: naive recursion → memoized recursion (caching collapses exponential to polynomial) → bottom-up DP (eliminating recursion overhead) → greedy (dropping subproblem tracking when local optimality guarantees global optimality), with each stage trading generality for efficiency.

justifications.label: Depth-3 synthesis connecting the recursion-DP bridge with the DP-greedy spectrum into a single four-stage pipeline

recursion-turing-complete.text: Recursion-only languages are Turing complete, equivalent in computational power to imperative languages with loops.

recursion-universally-optimizable.text: Every recursive algorithm can be systematically optimized through the recursion elimination and memoization pipeline: single recursion converts to iteration, multiple recursion is tamed by memoization into polynomial DP, providing a universal pathway from naive exponential recursion to efficient computation.

justifications.label: The optimization pipeline requires referential transparency; impure recursive functions break caching

redblack-234-isomorphism.text: Red-black trees are structurally isomorphic to 2-3-4 trees: a 2-node maps to a black node, a 3-node to black with one red child, a 4-node to black with two red children; color flip corresponds to node split.

redblack-btree-binary-encoding.text: Red-black trees are binary encodings of 2-3-4 trees, which are B-trees of order 4: the seemingly arbitrary red-black invariants are direct consequences of B-tree structural constraints translated to binary form.

justifications.label: the isomorphism explains red-black rules as B-tree properties in disguise

redblack-complexity.text: Red-black trees provide O(log n) worst-case time for search, insert, and delete operations.

redblack-guaranteed-logarithmic.text: Red-black trees provide guaranteed O(log n) worst-case operations because the red-black invariants constrain the longest path to at most 2x the shortest, preventing BST degeneration.

justifications.label: red-black invariants eliminate the BST degeneration pathology

redblack-height-bound.text: In a red-black tree, the longest root-to-leaf path is at most twice the shortest, ensuring tree height h ∈ O(log n).

redblack-history.text: Red-black trees were invented by Guibas and Sedgewick in 1978, evolving from Bayer's symmetric binary B-trees (1972).

redblack-insert-red.text: New nodes in a red-black tree are inserted as red to preserve black-height; this may create a red-red violation requiring rebalancing.

redblack-invariants.text: Red-black tree invariants: (1) every node is red or black, (2) all null nodes are black, (3) no red node has a red child, (4) every root-to-null path has the same number of black nodes.

redblack-practical-engineering-efficienc.text: Red-black trees achieve practical engineering efficiency through three implementation properties: red-only insertion preserves black-height requiring only recoloring in the common case, bounded rotations (at most 2 for insert, 3 for delete) keep structural modification costs predictable, and 1-bit color storage exploits pointer alignment for zero space overhead.

justifications.label: Three orphaned red-black implementation details combine into a unified practical efficiency claim

redblack-rotation-bounds.text: Red-black tree insert requires at most 2 rotations and delete requires at most 3 rotations; recoloring is O(log n) worst-case but O(1) amortized.

redblack-space-overhead.text: Red-black tree color storage costs 1 bit per node; in practice this can be zero by exploiting pointer alignment.

robertson-seymour-theorem.text: The Robertson-Seymour theorem states that every graph property closed under minors and subgraphs has a finite set of forbidden minors characterizing it

segtree-canonical-subset.text: Each node v in a segment tree stores in its canonical subset all input intervals that span Int(v) but do not span Int(parent(v)). Key lemma: any interval appears in at most two canonical subsets at the same tree depth.

segtree-complexity.text: Segment tree: O(n log n) build time, O(n log n) storage, O(log n + k) stabbing query time (k = reported intervals). Insert one interval costs O(log n). Counting variant uses O(n) storage with O(log n) query.

segtree-definition.text: A segment tree stores a set of intervals and answers stabbing queries: given a point, report all intervals containing it. It is a balanced binary tree over elementary intervals induced by the sorted endpoints of the input segments.

segtree-elementary-intervals.text: Elementary intervals partition the real line into alternating open intervals between consecutive endpoints and closed single-point intervals at endpoints, yielding at most 4n+1 elementary intervals for n segments. Single points are separate because query answers can differ at endpoints vs interiors.

segtree-higher-dimensions.text: Multi-level segment trees generalize to d dimensions, storing axis-aligned hyperrectangles with O(n log^d n) storage and O(log^d n) query time. Fractional cascading saves a log factor in query time; using an interval tree at the deepest level saves a log factor in storage.

segtree-history.text: The segment tree was invented by Jon Bentley in 1977 in 'Solutions to Klee's rectangle problems.'

segtree-not-cp-segtree.text: A segment tree, as defined in the antecedent, stores a set of intervals and answers stabbing queries: given a point, report all intervals containing it. It is built as a balanced binary tree over elementary intervals induced by the sorted endpoints of the input segments. This definition addresses interval storage and point-query retrieval rather than range aggregate operations.

segtree-storage-proof.text: Segment tree O(n log n) storage follows from: each interval stored at most twice per depth level (canonical subset lemma) × O(log n) tree height × n intervals.

segtree-vs-interval-tree.text: Segment trees use O(n log n) storage vs interval trees' O(n) for the same 1-D stabbing query problem. The segment tree's advantage is that canonical subsets can use any associated data structure, enabling clean generalization to higher dimensions where interval trees have no natural extension.

sentinel-node-purpose.text: A sentinel (dummy) node added before the first or after the last element of a linked list eliminates null-check edge cases in algorithms, trading extra space for simpler code — a poor tradeoff when many short lists exist.

separate-chaining-load-range.text: Separate chaining allows load factor α > 1 with optimal α_max between 1 and 3; performance degrades gradually with no hard failure point unlike open addressing

set-adt-definition.text: A set is an abstract data type that stores a collection of distinct values with no particular ordering; its primary operation is membership testing, not element retrieval by index.

set-as-map-with-dummy-values.text: A set can be implemented as an associative array (map) where keys are the set elements and values are a sentinel (e.g., 1 or unit type); conversely, a set is a map where the value type is the unit type.

set-bit-array-integer-subsets.text: Bit array implementation for sets that are subsets of integers 1..n supports O(1) membership test and very efficient union/intersection via bitwise operations.

set-bst-complexity.text: Self-balancing BST implementation of a set (e.g., red-black, AVL) provides O(log n) for most operations and additionally supports sorted iteration.

set-fold-requires-associative-commutativ.text: The fold operation on a set requires the combining function F to be both associative and commutative, because the iteration order over set elements is arbitrary and unspecified.

set-hash-consistency-contract.text: A set hash function must satisfy the consistency contract: if equal(S1, S2) then hash(S1) = hash(S2).

set-hash-table-complexity.text: Hash table implementation of a set provides O(1) average-case and O(n) worst-case time for membership test, add, and delete operations.

shortest-path-complete-performance-taxon.text: The shortest path algorithms covered by the available evidence can be partially characterized along two dimensions: a paradigm dimension, where greedy algorithms (Dijkstra, Prim) are significantly influenced by PQ implementation choice—with heap selection affecting whether the algorithm is queue-dominated or edge-dominated—while DP-based algorithms (Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall) have performance governed by exhaustive relaxation passes across edges; and a negative-weight dimension, where Dijkstra is excluded and the classical options reduce to Bellman-Ford for single-source (O(|V|·|E|)) or Floyd-Warshall for all-pairs (O(|V|³)).
